I will state one fact to show how keen the cannery men are that only their side of the case shall be given to the minister, and nothing given to members of parliament or others who are interested. In 1931 I endeavoured to learn what the canners were doing, and, hearing that the Deputy Minister of Fisheries -was to meet them in Vancouver I made it my business to go there and sit in at the meeting. It was held on a Saturday afternoon. The room was full of cannery men. I asked the deputy minister if he had any objection to my sitting in, and he said no. But when I walked in to the meeting you should have seen the look of consternation on the faces of those canners. Their hair almost stood on end. I said: "Gentlemen, I might just as well tell you who I am. I happen to be the member for New Westminster representing the fishermen of the Fraser river, and I am interested in this industry. I have heard the fishermen s side and now I want to hear the canners' side." One canner got up and said: "Mr. Deputy Minister, I thought this was a private meeting." It became so embarrassing that they did not know what to do. One member said: "I suggest that Mr. Reid go out of the room until we discuss this question." I went out and took my hat and coat and went off; as a member of parliament I was not going to stand waiting like a flunkey outside the door of a canners' meeting. That is the trouble: the deputy minister goes out there and meets the canners and gets an earful from them, and they come to Ottawa and give him another earful and then he holds a meeting with the fishermen. But until such time as a deputation of the fishermen and a deputation of the canners meet together with him on common ground this matter will never be satisfactorily settled. I would welcome the bringing from the Pacific coast of representatives of the canners' interests as well as those of the fishermen. I think now is the time that the whole matter should be gone into.
I was very sorry to hear the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) say: "I am in favour of this but I do not like the way the hon. member introduced it." Next time perhaps I shall consult him first when I am going to introduce a bill. But, Mr. Speaker, the fact is that if I had introduced this by

way of resolution he and a few of his friends might have talked it out and to-day we would find it at the foot of the order paper and so it would never be heard from again. I knew their tricks and their manners, and I introduced it as I did so that it would come squarely before the government. I speak as I feel in this matter because the livelihood of over 2,000 fishermen is at stake; they are threatened with being driven out by the vested interests who control and own most of the seines. I deprecate the acting minister giving the direction to the committee that the government is not going to accept the principle of the bill. maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night I was about to compare the Prime Minister's radio addresses with his previous speeches during the years from 1931 to 1934 in which he had pictured in glowing terms the steady return of prosperity to the Dominion of Canada. But those pictures glowing as they were, were as nothing compared with the full-

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Gray
page advertisement of the new Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hanson) published on the morning of January 2, entitled "Canadian Cavalcade." Hon. gentlemen will recall that it was on the evening of that same day that the Prime Minister commenced his radio broadcast. Reading that advertisement in the morning, and then tuning in the radio at night to listen to the Prime Minister's first address, is it any wonder that Canadians listened with amazement as they heard the Prime Minister of Canada in his opening remarks say: "This is a critical hour in the history of our country. The signs of recovery are few and doubtful. The signs of trouble are many, and they do not lessen." Someone listening to that broadcast and having read the previous speeches of the right hon. the Prime Minister was reminded of those words of Goldsmith:
Words of learned length and thundering sound
Amazed the gazing rustics ranged around';
And still they gazed, and still the wonder grew.
And still the wonder grew, Mr. Speaker, as his listeners heard the Prime Minister in that radio address once more denounce the dole. "I am against the dole," he said, "it mocks our claim to progress."
We awaited subsequent addresses to see just what the Prime Minister had in mind to substitute for the dole. My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) last night gave some figures showing the exact number of unemployed in Canada to-day. The Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Perley) said that we should not give those figures, that it would hurt the credit of Canada; but I say to him as I say to this house that it is time that the people of Canada knew the exact state of affairs; it is time that this national government gave some leadership to the dominion, and it is much better that we should know these facts and figures and have them on record in order that the people may realize the exact state of affairs if we are going to go on having municipalities default in interest payments and provinces struggling along on the verge of bankruptcy.
In November, 1934 we had on direct relief in this dominion something over 1,000,000 people. We had in December, 1934, 1,107,000 people on relief, and we had in January of this year 1935, 1,183,962 people on direct relief in this dominion.
His listeners were amazed to hear the Prime Minister once again declare that he would end unemployment. We .listened, all of us, interested to see what the Prime Minister might bring forth to end this all-important 92582-77
problem. We have had some legislation brought down, which I have not the time to review here. We have had unemployment insurance, and it has been shown I think conclusively that it will not assist those who are unemployed to-day, and that even those who are employed will not share in its benefits until at least some two years have elapsed. We have had the question of the minimum wage and the hours of labour, but there is not anything radical in a forty-eight hour week. In my own city of Sarnia we have had for some t.wo years, in a plant employing some 1,700 men, a forty hour week and an eight hour day, and yet I hold in my hand a dispatch in the press of that city to-day showing that the relief costs of that city for unemployment have been fairly steady. They show that the relief costs in 1934 were greater than in 1933. There is nothing radical therefore or anything that will greatly take up the slack of unemployment in a maximum forty-eight hour working week.
Then we have had the question of the revision of the Old Age Pensions Act. We recall, all of us, that the Prime Minister in 1930 stated that the national government would pay the full 100 per cent of the old age pension. I grant that as time goes on it is quite possible that the Old Age Pensions Act may need some revision, but that is not legislation that is new, and do not forget, as this country will not forget, that it was the Liberal government of my right hon. leader that placed that act upon the statute books.
Then we heard the Prime Minister say that he would appoint an economic council. That is good in itself, but what in the world will an economic council do to cure the unemployment situation? Why come forward now with the appointment of an economic council when for the last four or five years the Prime Minister has consistently refused the suggestion of my right hon. leader that a national council be set up to study the whole unemployment question in cooperation with the provinces and municipalities? Then we had fully one-half of a radio speech in which the Prime Minister said that he would abolish the no par value stock. That is rather strange coming from him at a time when, only a few months ago, a motion made by my hon. friend from Last Mountain (Mr. Butcher) was turned down by this very government. But does he think that the abolition of no par value stock will help the unemployment situation or touch the fringe of the dangers which he hopes to prevent in connection with speculations in company promotions? No; these things, good as they may be, do not

Unemployment Reliej-Mr. Gray

begin to get at the fundamentals of the situation. My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre last night quoted from the actuarial report prepared by Mr. Wolfenden in which he set out the causes of unemployment. Mr. Wolfenden, in gathering the data necessary to prepare this report, went into all the facts surrounding the question of unemployment; and when one reads the reasons he gives as the basis for his report to the Prime Minister, the reasons for the causes of unemployment in Canada, one finds that it is one of the greatest indictments of the policies of this government since its inception, and that the Prime Minister stands indicted to-day before the bar of public opinion on the strength of that report.
I am supporting this resolution, which is purely and simply a motion of want of confidence in the government, because I believe that the people of this country have lost confidence in hon. gentlemen opposite. That is evidenced not only by the by-elections that have taken place since 1932 but by the fact that the leader of the government has even lost faith in himself.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen may draw
their own conclusions, but speaking in Toronto on Saturday last the Prime Minister said that the election will come like a thief in the night. This was an address given to the young Canadian Conservative Clubs of Canada. I doubt whether the illustration was a very apt one coming from the Prime Minister to these young Canadians, but I will let that pass. The Prime Minister has always told us that he means exactly what he says. Well then, if he means exactly what he says in this statement, he is afraid to face the people in the open and will come with his election like a thief in the night. Let me say this to the Prime Minister, that the people of Canada have learned to protect themselves since 1930 and that he will not steal this election.
My time is almost up and I will not go into questions which might easily be raised in reference to what can be done towards solving this all-important problem that faces us. The Prime Minister said as recently as a week ago last Saturday that he knows the answer to the question. Speaking in New York on February 16, in an address to the Canadian Society, he made this statement:
I would find it impossible to conceive and develop a scheme of recovery and reform unless I first had definitely decided upon the answer to it.

If the right hon. gentleman has the answer, if he knows what the solution is for the problem that we are faced with, it is not contained in these radio addresses, splendid as they were from the oratorical point of view. If the right hon. gentleman has the answer-and he says he has-then in the name of everything that is just and right let him give that answer to-day to the people of Canada.
Hon. RAYMOND D. MORAND (East Essex): Yesterday we witnessed a member of the guard on the other side trying to blow a bit of fire back into the dying embers of the Liberal party. He used the bellows to the best possible advantage, but unfortunately the embers were cold, and they fell rather on useless and burned out ashes. I was rather surprised that a new leader had come forward with a policy and ideas of his own- pious wishes it would be better to say-as to how this great problem can be solved. He was unsupported by the Napoleon of the party, who I see is in his seat to-day; nor was the Marshal Ney of the party, the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), there to support him. I wonder if it is a plan projected, that he and those who are supporting him .to-day shall parade from one end of Canada to the other appealing to those to whom his particular type of oratory and that particular type of call which he is making has an appeal, leaving free his leaders to remain with the laissez-faire class that will help them to put over the election. With that amount of fire and vim he always puts into his speeches, when he began yesterday I had hoped that he would bring some new fuel to the dying embers. I had hoped that possibly he had something to hand to the Canadian people, the unemployed of this country, something that would bring them some solace and help. But he just added another regret to that litany of regrets which we have heard from the opposition benches during the last five years.
It is interesting to read the amendment to the resolution as submitted by the hon. member. His amendment reads:
That all the words after the word "That" in the motion be struck out, and the following substituted therefor:
This house regrets that, notwithstanding the specific promises made prior to the election of 1930, and many times since reiterated, and despite the fact that extraordinary powers to deal with unemployment have been repeatedly secured from parliament, the present administration, after nearly five years of office, has not yet submitted to parliament any definite or

Unemployment Reliej-Mr. Morand
effective policy to deal with widespread' actual unemployment or distress which continues to he Canada's most urgent national problem.
I am sure that will be some comfort to the unemployed of Canada. For five years I have listened to members on the other side; for five years I have hoped that possibly, with plenty of time on their hands and with the experience they have had, they might suggest some constructive bit of advice to these on this side in working out the problems that face this country; for five years I have hoped that possibly they would hold out the hand of cooperation and of help to assist Canada in solving this great problem. But they have consistently, from the very beginning, found more solace in the difficulties of the government than in their desire to help. I heard repeated again yesterday that same line which they hope to get across to the public-the supposedly broken promises of the Prime Minister. Why, they laugh at it themselves. One could repeat it almost without notes; bon. gentlemen opposite have reiterated it so often. But it is sometimes necessary to see clearly before you can remove the beam from your own eyes. I wonder if any of the members opposite have read the platform of 1919. I wonder if any of them know what was in that platform. I wonder if any of them have read the resolution?

3.	The payment to the employed of a wage adequate to maintain a reasonable standard of life as this is understood in their time and count ry.
4.	The adoption of an eight hour day or a forty-eight hour week as the standard to be aimed at where it has not already been attained.

But this is the gem:
That in so far as may be practicable, having regard for Canada's financial position, an adequate system of insurance against unemployment, sickness, dependence in old age. and other disability, which would include old age pensions, widows' pensions, and maternity benefits should be instituted' by the federal government in conjunction with the governments of the several provinces; and on matters pertaining to the industrial and social legislation an effort should be made to overcome any question of jurisdiction between the dominion and the provinces by effective cooperation between the several governments.
That was in 1919. We have listened to hon. members opposite talk about the wonderful prosperity that prevailed under their regime. We have heard them talk about the wonderful financial conditions that existed during their term of office and about the wonderful cooperation they had with the provinces. Despite that, we find ourselves at this late stage with all of this program unfulfilled and no attempt made to fulfil it. Some attempt has been made to say that because the Senate was opposed, these schemes were not put into effect, but I can remember the welkin ringing with the phrase Reform the Senate." The Liberal party was nine years in power, but the Senate remained unreformed. When we hear hon. gentlemen opposite day after day recalling the broken promises of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett); when we realize the condition of the country during his term of office and

compare it with conditions that exist throughout the world, and when they are to-day confronted with a list of unfulfilled promises such as those I have cited, never again should we hear from the other side talk about broken promises on the part of the Prime Minister.
Yesterday I heard the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) finding fault with many of the works that had been accomplished by this government. For instance, I heard him find fault with the wheat control. I wonder whether those in the prairie provinces who were able with the help of the government to maintain the price of wheat at the point they did will welcome the criticism leveled at that piece of work. I wonder whether the railroad workers who were retained at work because of advances to the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National will consider this was an improper spending of money in order to keep the railway shops open.
During yesterday's discussion we had a reiteration of the nine points that were submitted during the last five years, those nine points that are supposed now to be the new chart of the Liberal party. .

I wonder just how much help that would be to the unemployed. We have had four such conferences already and in regard to two provinces we know only too well their financial situation.
2.	That unemployment was Canada's most urgent national problem, and strongly advocated a representative national commission to coordinate all national effort and to cooperate with the provinces and municipalities in the administration of unemployment relief.
Do the unemployed of this country complain of the way in which the relief has been handled?

with that, but I am satisfied that the relief work that has been done for the unemployed has been done as well as it could have been by any central administration. Surely those in the municipalities who know the unemployed, who are close to them, are in a much better position to take care of them than any one commission such as suggested in this clause with central headquarters could have done.
3.	That there should' be an audit by the federal government of all expenditure of public moneys.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
During the entire speech
of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre yesterday and of the hon. member for West Lambton, did we hear a single word of commendation or praise for the work that has been done by this government? Did we hear them mention any good that came from the Ottawa agreements, any good that came from the public works undertaken throughout this whole dominion to give work to the unemployed? Did we hear them comment favourably upon the way relief was handled? Did we hear them say anything in commendation of the marketing bill, of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, of the Canadian farm loan board, of the eight-hour day, of the unemployment insurance measure and amendments to the Companies Act? Had they anything good to say of the work, started by
this government and now in process, of the price spreads and mass buying commission whose report is expected soon, or of the treaties with foreign nations, of the support of the wheat market, aid to the railway workers, the abolition of dumping that would have thrown our men out of work? To-day the Prime Minister and his government are amplifying this work already so well begun and are providing in the legislation now before the house and to be brought down a plan that will go still further and continue to help those in this country who are in difficulty. And what do we find? The first thing is an attack upon its constitutionality. I have heard that word ever since I came here in 1925. It won an election, I believe, in 1926 but I doubt that the people will again fall for constitutional issues.
One thing I resent is the attitude of the other side that they and they alone have sympathy for those who are in difficulty, that they and they alone are anxious about the unemployed, that they and they alone are looking for a way out. I believe that those on this side who are carrying the burden, those upon whose shoulders the responsibility falls, those who so unfairly are held accountable for conditions, have the fullest realization of what they have to do and what they should try to do, and I am satisfied that they will do it. When the people of this country are called upon to pass judgment upon these reform measures, these measures of amelioration, these advances in legislation, this progress, I wonder to whom they will turn. Will they turn to those who believe that these measures are the illegitimate children of a violated constitution, or will they turn to those who believe them constitutional and will father them and finish their work and carry this program through so that the Canadian people may resume their way towards the prosperity that they have a right to enjoy.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, throughout the course of several speeches we have been listening to the kettle calling the pot black or the pot calling the kettle black, whichever way one would put it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You call it red.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is not my purpose to enter into that aspect of the discussion. The amendment presented is I think one that we in this corner cannot avoid supporting, although I say frankly that I regret having to support an amendment bolstered up by such speeches as we had yesterday. The amendment states that:
1208	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Woodsworth
The present administration, after nearly five years of office, has not yet submitted to parliament any definite or effective policy to deal with widespread or actual unemployment or distress which continues to be Canada's most urgent national problem.
I agree with that statement. I think we may all admit that we have not had brought forward in the last five years anything that effectively deals with this problem.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Has any other country?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: An hon. gentleman says. Has any other country? No. I frankly admit that no country has altogether solved the problem, but I do say that some other countries have been more successful than we have.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Name them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Great Britain for one.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They have more unemployed in relation to population than we have.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, and further than that the point I wish to emphasize is that many of us do not believe that the problems are solvable under the existing capitalistic system. We say that frankly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go to Russia.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And we do not believe that we can justly hold either the Liberal party or the Conservative party wholly responsible for failing to solve these problems. They cannot do it under the system under which they are working. But we do say that as long as either of these parties clings to the existing system it is bound at least to take reasonable care of the citizens of this country. This the government so far has not_done. It is quite true that we are considering a provision for unemployment insurance which will help a certain limited group of people in a very inadequate fashion, but the Prime Minister himself has declared that this is not a relief policy and will not assist any of those now unemployed. Nor has the Prime Minister seen fit so far in this session to bring down any program dealing with the unemployment question. We in this corner have been patiently awaiting that program through the weeks that have passed, but there is no indication that any such statement is forthcoming. The Prime Minister has stated that he does not like the dole. None of us do. There is more than a suspicion that the government is seeking more and more to throw the responsibility for unemployment relief upon the provinces and municipalities, and that at a time
FMr. Woodsworth.]
when a good many of the municipalities are practically bankrupt. As I said the other day, I do not think we should let this parliament prorogue without having had placed before us a well thought out scheme for dealing with the actual situation which confronts us.
Sometimes I feel very weary indeed when year after year we have to bring up this question of unemployment. I think it was in 1922, some thirteen years ago, that I first introduced a motion on going into supply that something should be done with regard to unemployment, and year after year we have had to call the attention of the house to this same question. We have tried to point out the actual conditions throughout the country. We have tried to show the cost of unemployment. From time to time we have tried to analyze the economic conditions that lead to unemployment. We have tried to advance certain schemes, such as the housing scheme and others, which would seem to be a practical way of beginning to deal with this question. We have gone into the more fundamental matters and urged that unemployment is bound to remain with us as long as wre operate under this profit system. We have done all this. It is not my purpose to-day to go into the question of the constitutional responsibilities. Both sides of this house in turn have acknowledged that this is a national problem, and I think the government could not but receive support from all sides of the house if they were bold enough to initiate a thorough going national scheme for dealing with the present unemployment situation. I do not propose to go into the statistics of the matter; we have had statistics until our heads fairly swim with them. It is not statistics we want; it is action. I do not think even the supporters of the government will venture to say that there is anything before us yet or likely to come before us that will really solve this problem or affectively assist this large number of our unemployed fellow Canadian citizens.
I should like for a few minutes, if I might, to get away from the atmosphere of this house-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The door is not locked.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh, yes; someone
says the door is not locked and that we may go. It is very easy to make a joke of these things, but I earnestly ask hon. members of this house to allow me for a few minutes to try to make them realize what is involved in this unemployment question. I think, surely, every hon. member must know of

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Woodsworth
at least some cases, among his circle of friends, of those who have been affected or whose homes have been affected by unemployment. Surely there must have been individual cases in which hon. members have become interested, where they have seen how people who have been unemployed for years have become demoralized. I can quite understand that if this problem continues very much longer we may have an even greater degree of crime than has developed in the last few years. I can understand that we are going to have a very large measure of inefficiency among the young men who have never learned to work. I can understand that we are going to have restlessness among great sections of the population that will be very serious in character. But notwithstanding this we seem to drift on from year to year. In fact it was only the other day that someone in this house referred to the people in the unemployment relief camps as being almost useless to society, suggesting that they should not have the right even to participate in elections.
I submit that as yet we have not realized just what is involved. A few months ago in the west I picked up this item from the newspaper. A twenty-one year old boy from Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, seeking to board a train near Regina, fell between the moving cars and was seriously injured. This young chap apparently had a home down near Halifax. He had a sister but no mother. He had gone west in the hope of securing a job. He got as far as Moose Jaw and then tried to board a freight train. I suppose technically that is an offence against the law, yet it is the only way by which large numbers of our people can get from place to place. This young chap fell between the cars and was seriously injured. As the men came to lift him up and take him to the hospital he exclaimed, "Kill me. I am no good for anything now." The desperation of that young man is the desperation of a great many young fellows throughout the country to-day, and I want to say that if it were not for the fact that some of us had a little higher standard of living and some reserves the position of that boy would have been the position of some of our own boys to-day. I cannot look at my own boys without thinking what their future would be if they did not have a little extra help from home. There was this young man from the east, apparently, by his name, a French Canadian, trying to make his way, going to the west and now considered almost a useless part of our society. I suppose, according
to the Prime Minister's philosophy, God was not just as good to him as he was to the Prime Minister. I say that in all seriousness. I believe the Prime Minister's philosophy is an absolutely rotten philosophy. I want to say in all seriousness that if we are really reverent in our hearts we will recognize that young chaps like that have just as much right in Canada and just as much right to a full life in Canada as have the very foremost citizens of Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What did you know about that boy before that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nothing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then you are talking
about something you know nothing about.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
submit that if there is a question to be asked the hon. member should address the chair.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And ask the permission of the Minister of Finance.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I give that incident, Mr. Speaker, because in a somewhat dramatic way it brings before the house the essence of the problem we are facing. For a few moments I shall take the time of the house to read an article which I have had in my files for a couple of years. This article appeared in the Western Producer of September 28, 1933, and is signed by William George Rundle. I believe it is worth while to have one of these unemployed men address the house and tell us something of the problems they have to face.
I am in a relief camp. Penniless and homeless and destitute, I am one who is clothed and fed and housed by the government, and I am wondering what the -world is doing. I am one who vizualizes electrically lighted streets, glittering automobiles, theatre lights, bakery windows, softly lighted restaurants and' hears the soothing hum of conversation and the silvery peal of a woman's laughter. I am one apart and I am one of many.
Then, a little later on:
Who am I? I am a university graduate; behind me I have four years of university life and after my name I can write a degree. One of my friends-a fellow labourer-is a pharmacist, another a military engineer, another a medical student, another a school teacher-a former principal; another an artist-come to his tent and he will show you pastels, pen and ink sketches, hand engraved greeting cards and water colours of still life.
On all sides of me are men from every walk of life-the creeds and 'beliefs and religions of all nations. All nationalities, all the professions, all the trades and all the labouring divisions are gathered here.
1210	COMMONS
Unemployment Relic}-Mr. Woodsworth
We are complete. In our tent city set off in the Saskatchewan prairie we are a community to ourselves; we can cook; we can tailor; we can teach; we can fashion our own tools; we can design our own power plant and we can build it; we can lay out our own buildings and, those of us who are carpenters, can build them; we can lay out water mains and servers and our plumbers can construct them; we can fill our own prescriptions; we can keep our own accounts; we can type our own letters.
And then at a later point he states;
A train whistles in the distance. We see the smoke trailing off in the deep blue sky and we hear the rolling clink of metal upon metal as the wavering wisps of smoke trail northwards; cars hum on the highway and in our minds we hear the thud and crunching of rubber on gravel. They pass us by. We are beings who pause and' listen whilst behind the whispering line of poplars the world goes rolling by. Beyond is the life we have known;
And still later:
Above on our bell shaped canvas roofs we see slow moving grasshoppers clinging to the sloping sides and advancing to the peak of our frail shelter. Is there a lesson to be taken from the slow footed advance? Inevitably the grasshopper moves onward and upwards. Is it a sign? Are we to be patient and wait as we have waited through the years; through the first relief camp in 1931 and on to this, our third, in 1933?
He might very well have added, "Our fifth, in 1935." Then skipping a few paragraphs I read:
We are khaki clad men in army fatigue uniforms-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Take it as read.
board. They hope for better things; they look for better things but for the nonce they wag their heads wisely and remain silent.
Middle aged men gather and converse in low tones, vainly and desperately seeking "the way out," attempting to formulate new policies or find the weak link in our economic armour. There is no definite bitterness. We are beyond bitterness as the hopeless days pass-with a never-ending succession of hopeless days ahead. In place of bitterness there is a thoughtful consideration of reported world conditions, of the conditions of the crops and the movements of Mr. R. B. Bennett. There is no violence but a realization that something must be done.
Eyes stray to khaki trousers, army blankets, and army fatigue shirts. Is it to last forever? Are we to be "kept" all our lives?
There is impatience-yes! Perhaps lips move in a mental addition of the month's wages at twenty cents a day. And then a hopeless shrug,
Nerves are kept well under control or else there would be heard the wild, straining cry: "Oh God! what next?"
There comes a silence, each man thoughtfully smoking, chin upon hand and staring sightlessly ahead-lantern light, sharp shadows, bronzed cupped faces and the white outline of shimmering canvas. Another day is passing and another day will soon he dawning. "Oh God! what next?"
After describing the work of the frontier college instructors, he states:
The younger men are interested and some of them attend or form classes. The majority however are "stiffs." For years they have been on relief and bitterness, like a canker, has passed and left an ever present wound. Willing but unwanted! Desire has changed to apathy and apathy to brooding and' now the days are merely units that stretch as far back as the eye can see and as far ahead as the imagination can reach.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman says, "Take it as read." No, he is going to listen to this for the next ten minutes, if he stays in the chamber. I insist that this man be heard. He is the representative of tens of thousands of our fellow citizens:
We are khaki clad men in army fatigue uniforms and heavy steel-plated artillery boots, plodding to work through the shifting sand'. Our blankets are provided, and palliasses of straw, and our trousers and shirts, and socks and underwear, our shaving equipment and our towels and tooth brushes. We are numbers on a relief project, we rise, and work, and eat, and receive hospital treatment and retire to the sound of the bugle. Our day is mapped out for us. We follow definite rules. And we are numbered for equipment and record purposes.
Then in several paragraphs is contained a description of the routine of camp life. Following that he describes what occurs towards evening:
Old men congregate together. They seem satisfied and placidly look back over twenty years farming, discuss the trivial events of the day or perhaps they bend earnestly over a game of rummy, or sevens up, or a cribbage

then, as they are summoned to bed:
Is it in irony that the last post is played instead of lights out? The notes rise into the air and the stately, solemn sound sinks into each soul. Lamps go out. Voices are stilled.
The last note floats high into the air and dies m the rolling hills. We have become but a faint line of white and the prairie has folded over us, but within man upon man lies awake, ana stares stony-eyed into the darkness.
"Oh, God! what next?"
Some hon. members may have thought that I have no right to read this description in the House of Commons. I submit that there is as much sense in that article, and a great deal more insight than is shown on many occasions by what is said on the floor of this chamber. It represents a point of view that is too little heard here and which to-day I ask should be considered. At the risk of wearisome iteration may I be permitted to give another example which I 'believe fairly well illustrates the position in which thousands of people find themselves to-day. Some friends of mine whom I have known about fifteen years had come some years previously from Poland.

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Woodsworth
This man and his wife were exceptionally high types of settlers. Leaving their native village in Europe, because of the glowing pictures painted in those earlier days by our immigration representatives they were induced to come to this country. They came here hoping to make a home of their own, and were settled by the authorities at a point between the lakes, as we describe it, in northern Manitoba, on land which should never have been opened for settlement. They did not know the quality of the land and in all good faith they took a homestead. Year after year after year they worked on the homestead. They sold their butter and eggs at ridiculously low prices, really below the cost of production. They waded through almost impassable roads to get to the local village. They picked stones because the country was not unlike the country we sometimes see along the St. Lawrence where several generations ago the patient settlers picked stones off their lands. Unfortunately between the lakes, when they got the stone picked after unending toil, there was no soil that was worth anything much. For years they worked. They incurred debts, do as they would. The man went out to work, leaving his wife alone for long periods, and coming back with a little money to buy groceries. At last, having piled up debts and with no income coming in, with two young children to care for, they felt they could continue no longer, and they left their farm and came to live in the city.
Again let me say that this move is typical of that of hundreds of people whom we have in nearly all our cities in the west. The man was a skilled mechanic and found a place in the Canadian Pacific Railway shops. There he set to work with a will once more to try to make a home for his family. The wife was a very ambitious and capable woman. She went out working by the day in the hope that they might more quickly make a bit of money so that they might pay off their debts and give their children a chance. I used to know her in the days when she would go out to work hard all day and at night go to a public night school where the English language was taught. She wanted to be able to talk English fluently to her children as they grew up in this English country. They worked for some years before they were able to pay off the debts which they had contracted on the farm. It looked as if they were about to get into a position where they could be independent once more.
Then came the depression. I remember the man telling me that there were only a few ahead of him on the list to be let go. The
company was gradually displacing more and more men, and for months he was afraid that his turn to be laid off would come next. Finally the time did come and he lost his job. His wife did not find it quite so easy now to get work in her line. The depression grew worse. In the meantime they had attempted to buy a house in the city. Possibly at this distance we may say that they were foolish to make such an attempt, but they had saved several hundred dollars, a sufficient amount to make the first payment, and they had that longing and earnest desire which almost every man and woman has, to have a little home of theii own, and so they bought a house and began trying to make the payments on it.
Finally the man had to go on relief work, some work provided by the city, and while digging a ditch he was injured. There was no compensation for him because he was merely on relief work. He received a very bad blow in the head. He had to go to the hospital, which meant expense for himself and his wife.
By this time, the children had passed up through high school. The parents could not afford to send them on to university or to place them in any other school, so then they were taken out of school, with no work for either the boy or the girl.
Then came greater slackness of work, and bitterness of bitterness, they had actually to go on relief. These people who had been I suppose twenty-five years in Canada, who had worked long hours, who had tried to farm, who had tried industrial life, now were driven to accept relief from the city. They did it finally because they could do no other, and besides they hoped that in some way or other they might keep this home he last effort they would ever make to have a home of their own.
Sickness added to their difficulties. The man had to go to the hospital. He returned not cured physically, but worse than that he was mentally so dejected that his mind could hardly be said to be normal. I had lost track of the family for several years, but I came across them again a few months ago when they were in this condition. It was only a few weeks after, that one morning at an early hour a trackman walking along the Canadian Pacific Railway tracks found the man dead beside the tracks. In some way he had been struck by the engine. Then came the great expense of the funeral, which is no small expense in a working man's family, especially when the people are on relief. The woman, one of the most efficient women that I have met, a woman who if brought up in another circle would be fit to occupy almost
1212	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Woodsworth
any position, was prematurely aged, broken in spirit. Her two children bom in Canada and to-day about twenty years of age, bright, well-trained young people but with no work to do. The girl received a few weeks' work during the Christmas rush at one of the department stores, all she has had for months, although trained to do good work.
Now, Mr. Speaker, and if it were proper. I should like almost to say, Miss Maephail and gentlemen of the House of Commons, I have recited that case to show the situation that to-day faces hundreds of thousands of our fellow-Canadians. There are just one or two points that I would like to leave with this house. One is that these people are idle through no fault of their own. There are a few lazy people-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why did the United Farmers of Manitoba pass a resolution asking for the abolition of the unemployment camps It was so that they could get men to work on the farms. The trouble is you have them crowding into the cities and you cannot get them out on the land.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I ask the hon. member to please answer that question: Why did the organization which he knows very well, that belongs to Manitoba, pass a resolution asking for the abolition of the unemployment camps?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman wants to ask a question, he will kindly do so without argument.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I cannot accept responsibility for any resolution passed by the United Farmers of Manitoba. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is clear that although there may be some lazy people and some shiftless people, some misfits, I think it must be conceded that the great majority of our unemployed to-day have become unemployed simply because no job was available for them. That is the outstanding fact we ought not to lose sight of.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is plenty of work on the farms.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not intend to be diverted by the interjections of my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Mullins) except to say that there is not plenty of work on the farms to-day at anything like a living wage.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, a good living.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, there is not, and there is no use talking about it. The farmer cannot pay his men. I tried to get young fellows placed on farms last summer, but I found that farmers would not pay them even their board.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the remedy?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Never mind the
remedy for the moment; I am pointing out the situation that exists. I quite admit that a number of these people who have been for years unemployed will shortly become unemployable; there is no doubt about that, but that is not the question under discussion. It is true that we are manufacturing these people by our present policies. But the real question is what are we going to do about the entire unemployment situation?
There is another point I want to leave with the house, and it too is incontrovertible. It is this, that the people who are idle through no fault of their own have a claim for adequate maintenance. I do not suggest that they should be sent to a farm to work for nothing and pay their own board; I do not suggest that they should be sent to relief camps-bright young fellows such as the one that wrote that article in The Producer- to work for twenty cents a day. That method is a disgrace, and anyone with any spirit in him will protest against that kind of treatment.
If the governments of the provinces and the government of the dominion, with all the resources which they have for surveying the situation, with all the resources at their command, cannot find jobs for these people, then the least that they can do is to give them adequate maintenance, a good living. I do not mean five cent meals, or twenty cents a day; I mean, in the case of single men, enough to enable them to secure three meals a day, a good clean bed, and enough to provide themselves with decent clothing so that they can hold up their heads in the world; and in the case of men with families, that they be provided, not with a tumble down shelter where they can scrape up a sort of existence, dependent upon charity for clothes and medical assistance, but some sort of pension, if you want to call it that, whereby they can draw a certain amount regularly, weekly or monthly, from the government, a sum sufficient to maintain them and their children in decency and to educate their children and give them a chance in life. I think that is undoubtedly the duty of this parliament.
You may object that we cannot afford to do that; you say that it would spoil these

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Rinfret
people if they were given these things for nothing. I do not want to give a living to them for nothing, but I do urge that as decent Canadians they are entitled to a decent living. If we did give it to them I do not think it would take very long before we devised ways and means of finding something for them to do. That is quite proper. Every man has a right to contribute to society, but in the meantime these people ought to be kept. I do not expect that the present government is going to overturn the capitalistic system, notwithstanding all the Prime Minister has said. But if this system is one that is fundamentally sound, as the Prime Minister asserts, and only needs a little bit of reform, then the least we can do with the unemployed is to see that they are adequately supported.
Further I think we are right in throwing upon the government the responsibility of devising ways and means. This is in accordance with the very best constitutional practice. We have suggested from this comer certain things which we think would materially assist. We say for instance that there might be a very extensive housing program, which would help greatly. We say that instead of having this financed by borrowed money it should be financed through the credit of the country, without increasing interest or debt. And that is quite possible. Some one may denounce that as inflation but inflation of that sort would be a good thing for Canada at the present time. I do not mean uncontrolled inflation. If France can bring her franc down from twenty cents to four cents with advantage to most of her people, I cannot see why Canada cannot do the same with her dollar. We have pointed out further in this comer that there are certain fundamental financial changes that will have to be made. Perhaps the system will not stand the extra load that such a program as I have suggested would place upon it; but on the other hand I do not think that the system as it exists to-day will stand very much longer the strain that is being put upon it by the present government or would be put upon it by any otheT government that seeks to uphold the capitalist system. However, I do not want to get off into a discussion of these things. I think that if the government is right in saying that the people have entrusted them with responsibility-and the Prime Minister has insisted on this time time and again-then undoubtedly it is their responsibility to handle this situation. And we stand ready to do the very best we can to assist.
But I -want to come back to the plea I am trying to make in this speech, if you can call it a speech. I ask that we for a little while get away from the political game that is played here day in and day out, week in and week out, year in and year out, and consider the seriousness of the situation that faces us in Canada. Do you think that these million of people on relief to-day can go on as they are going now very much longer? Is there any sign of a real letup in this depression? What shall we do in the next year or two or three years? How can we expect to have these people remain loyal and few abiding? I want to know what claim this government has upon the loyality of people who do not get even enough to enable them to live in decency? I would go this far: I should like to know what claim any system of democracy has upon its citizens when that democracy does not enable them to supply themselves even with the necessities of life. I warn this house, we cannot go on in this way very much longer, and I do urge that from this time on, in this session, we give the most serious consideration to this very pressing problem.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I rise to support the amendment. I am glad to have heard the leader of the group in the corner say that he would support it. Although I do not agree with his views on capitalism and other matters, I fully agree with the picture he has given to-day of the unemployment situation in this country. I think he has given some very impressive examples of destitution amongst our people. I was sorry to see that occasionally what he said did not meet with that degree of sympathy which it should get from the house, but I am in agreement with him when he says that notwithstanding anything before the house now, unemployment remains essentially the problem that should engage our attention.
The amendment is quite concise and clear. It might be divided into three distinct parts. In the first- place, it reminds the house of specific promises made prior to the election of 1930. Secondly, it reminds the house of the extraordinary powers to deal with unemployment that have been repeatedly secured from this parliament by the present government. And in the third place, comparing these promises with the full powers that were given the government to redeem them, it reminds the house that nothing specific has been done to meet the tremendous problem that exists. We are not to be surprised that the people are so disappointed to-day in view of the lack of policy of the government in this respect. When the Prime Minister delivered his now
1214	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Rinjret
famous addresses over the radio at New Year's, the people regarded these addresses as an earnest effort to solve the deplorable conditions that exist at the present time, and it is not to be wondered at that, finding out that the whole program of reform on the part of the government is not for to-day but for to-morrow or next year or five years hence, the people who are unemployed feel that they have been completely overlooked in the new program.
We have on the order paper measures concerning social legislation, but what is social legislation to people who are not working? How can you interest them in a project which does not concern them and is dealing only with a condition that may arise not any sooner than a couple of years hence? There is on on the order paper a measure for limiting the hours of work, but what is that to people who do not work at all? Their hours of work are limited in the extreme and naturally a reform of this kind, even if good in itself, cannot bring any relief to them. On the order paper there is another measure to provide for a weekly day of rest, but again I ask: What does that mean to men who not only rest one day in the week but are forced to rest for the whole seven days? We are told that later on we shall have a measure to regulate wages. Again I ask:	What is
that to a man who, not having any wages at all, does not expect to benefit by this kind of legislation?
But if I have been impressed by the speech delivered by my good friend the leader of the Labour party (Mr. Woodsworth), I shall say in all frankness that I was less impressed by the speech delivered by the hon. member for East Essex (Mr. Morand). If he speaks for his party, may I for a moment dwell upon the great change in the tone of the speeches that we are having from the Conservative party to-day and those that we heard in 1930 and the first years of this parliament? In 1930 the Conservatives were claiming that the then Liberal government had done no good with regard to labour, but that if the Tories were returned to power, they alone, and sometimes the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) insinuated that he alone, would solve the problem of unemployment. I remember very well in one of the first sessions of this parliament when from this side of the house a motion similar to this was moved and the government was asked why they were not going on with the solution of that problem. Again the Prime Minister said: Give me health and a term of office and I will solve that problem. He was going to do it and his government was going to do it. But what

do we hear now from tho hon. member for East Essex? He says that if the government has not solved the unemployment problem, it is because the Liberals have failed to cooperate. In other words, after defeating us by contending that we could not solve the problem, this government are now trying to put the blame on us because they have not been able to achieve a solution themselves. I am not mentioning this from a strictly political standpoint as I might be accused of doing by certain hon. gentlemen, but I say that the government is at fault because not only did it disregard every project submitted by hon. members in the comer to my left and every resolution submitted by ourselves, but. it did not seek cooperation. The government claimed unlimited powers for itself in the form of a blank cheque; it told the house and the country: We do not need the opposition; we do not wish to discuss the matter with parliament; we have no regard for the Progressive party; give us unlimited power, vote that blank cheque and we will do everything ourselves. That is what took place But now we are on the eve of an election and the government says:	We did not do it
because the Liberals did not help us to do it. If this government wants our cooperation, I think the electorate is even much more anxious than is the government to have the cooperation of the Liberal party and it will prove that at the earliest possible opportunity Another claim that is made is that when we raise the question of unemployment we are obstructing the work of the house. We shall certainly hear that before this debate is over. I do not recall in all my short experience as a member of parliament and in earlier years as a member of the press gallery an opposition making such generous and complete offers of cooperation to a government as we have done this year. We have waived completely our right to take part in the debate on the address; we have waived private members' motions for a number of sittings; we are even ready to give assurance to the government that if they will not press any motion for supply, we will make it easy for them later on to get all the supply they need. What we wanted to do-and I wish to say that again to the hon. member for East Essex-was to cooperate with the government if it would only bring down its famous reforms. We have had them and I am going to make a frank statement to the house and the country: we are supporting those reforms in principle; there are some details upon which we are not agreed. I will say further: If I were to listen to some opposition in the part of the country from which I come

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Rinjret
I would sometimes hesitate to give my unlimited support to those measures; yet in a spirit of cooperation, of political abnegation to a certain extent, because we believe in the principles of those reforms and because we want to give the government the fullest cooperation in carrying out those measures, we will support unemployment insurance and other reform measures and I am ready to vote for them although quite a number of my electorate wants me to vote the other way. So far as cooperation is concerned, is that good faith on our part? I wish to emphasize that I think the comment the hon. member made to-day is altogether undeserved.
When we raise the question of unemployment that is not lack of cooperation; it is not obstruction. We believe it is the more pressing problem before the country and parliament. We believe in framing this program of reform the Prime Minister has overlooked the essential thing-how to remedy not future but present conditions. The diseased body is given a preventive against future sickness, but there is no remedy for the present one and the government is just like a doctor who would tell a patient: well, if you do not die from the present disease, I promise to cure you for the next one that you may contract. We are asking the government: Before you insure against unemployment of the year 1938 or 1939 and before you limit hours of work and set a wage scale for those who still enjoy the privilege of working, give a little more thought to those who are at present unemployed, to those who have no hours of work, no wages and who have to depend entirely on provincial and municipal aid. If we insist on that, it is because the government, far from indicating that it will at this session introduce legislation to cure unemployment, is now receding from the very limited degree of help that it has given to the provinces in the past. In June, 1934, at the end of the session the government through the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) announced that it might abandon its contribution to direct relief. Later on there took place in Ottawa a conference, a sham conference I would call it, which lasted exactly three days. One day was consecrated to welcoming the premiers from the different parts of the country and of course the last day was consecrated to wishing them goodbye when they were returning home; there was only one day of conference, and what took place? There was no discussion, no debate, no opportunity even for any of those premiers to present their case, but merely an ultimatum from the Prime Minister that they would be told later on what this government was willing to do.
And what took place as regards the province of Quebec? This government was paying, or at least was supposed to pay, one-third of the relief money and other unemployment money. That amounted to over a million dollars I am sure. The Minister of Labour notified Hon. Mr. Taschereau that in future it would be only 8600,000, and since then it has fallen to $500,000 and I think it is now only 8400,000, and it is my observation that even that small amount of money is very hard to get from the federal government; you must send in accounts, and other accounts, and have them checked north and checked south, and the government has always been six or eight months late in its payments. But I do not want to discuss that part of it, I see I am disturbing the minister already.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? I do not like to interrupt, and I rarely do, but there was no time that the federal government was ever six or eight months behind in payments to the province of Quebec.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not a question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But the province of Quebec has been eighteen months behind in sending in their accounts for payment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, here we have an admission of delay, whether it was due to my hon. friend or to the province. Whatever money the federal government pays to the municipalities is not only being reduced all the time but payment is subject to considerable delay. Let me point out that I read in the paper this morning that for the month of March the municipal administration of Montreal is asked to vote 81,443,771, nearly a million and a half dollars. If the federal government is going to contribute not one-third, but merely $400,000 to the whole province, you will see that it means a very paltry sum indeed as the city of Montreal's proportion. Yet there was a time when the government was willing to pay one-third, so I am quite right in saying that not only is the present government not coming forward with any help or policy in the matter of unemployment, but on the contrary is receding considerably.
The government was not very ready to discuss this problem with the provincial premiers in 1934, or to discuss it with the mayors. I remember that not a month ago we were told through the newspapers that this government had declined to receive in Ottawa a delegation of mayors, and I am surprised

Unemployment Rekej-Mr. Rinjret
that it was not anxious to meet even the mayor of Montreal. I think it should have been pleased to meet him. It was not very anxious to meet me sometimes when I was mayor. But I am pointing out that we have only omissions to underline in the matter of a policy by this government in regard to unemployment. They did not accept the offer of the premier of Quebec. Correspondence was laid on the table on February 15 on the motion of the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) showing that a generous offer was received from Hon. Mr. Taschereau; at least it was something positive. He said the province was willing to pay 50 per cent if the federal government would pay 50 per cent. The statement of the Minister of Labour was that the offer was not made in good faith, that the premier of Quebec knew very well that this government would not accept it. Well, why not test the sincerity of the premier of Quebec, why not accept the offer if only to find out whether Mr. Taschereau would live up to his part? I think Mr. Taschereau was very sincere in making that offer, but that the Minister of Labour was much more sincere when he refused. That part of the transaction at least is very clear.
Besides that we have had a slackening in public works. Look at the city of Montreal for instance. Not a veTy large amount of money was voted for Montreal out of the famous S40,000.000 program, but there was something, mostly it is true for the western part, where- the vote is more likely to be on the sid-e of the Conservative party; yet we are interested in public works all over the city. But they have not been going on very rapidly. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I may tell you that the public works policy of this government in my city is a policy of excavations. We had the excavation of the Canadian National Railways terminal some years ago; there it is, gaping wide open to the view o>f the public. Later on we heard that my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) -not from himself, because he never wants to give any information on that matter, but through the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart)-was going to build a postal terminal in Montreal. Well, the land was excavated a couple of years ago, and there it gapes, a true companion to the Canadian National excavation.
