speechtext: With a fence around.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was told a few days ago that contracts had 'been let and that at last this terminal would be built. I regret that inasmuch as this government decided to
TMr. Rinfret.]
supplement what it was not doing in direct relief by public works, it has not been more expeditious as regards works in Montreal.
Another cause for grave apprehension is as to what is going to take place after the first of April. The other day -the Minister of Labour in replying to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) said something that is most extraordinary, but if it indicates anything it indicates that the government itself does not know what it will do after the first of April. Here is what the Minister of Labour said:
I do not know' that I made the announcement that direct relief would terminate on March 31, but this government is keeping in close touch with the provinces and a decision will be arrived at as to what method may have to be employed with respect to assisting them. Up to the moment v'e have not had any information or request from the provinces as to what assistance they may need.
I do not wish to be unfair, I will admit that in that reply there is an indication of some intention on the part of the government to do something, but it is a cause of gravest concern to all interested parties to see that hesitancy and evident lack of decision in so essential a matter.
The unemployment question is a national problem. I may again refer to the quotation made by the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Gray) from an order in council passed by this government in 1931, P.C. 2043:
Whereas unemployment is primarily a municipal and provincial responsibility, it has been so general throughout Canada as to constitute a national concern.
On that I think we are all agreed, and I hope -one of the decisions of this government wil be not to abandon that attitude as regards unemployment. It is a problem for this government and this parliament primarily to solve. There is good ground for that attitude, because after all, while seasonal and local unemployment may be due to local conditions, when we have a general state of unemployment as we have in Canada now we can say it is due primarily to the condition of trade and industry in the country. I do not say that 'by changing one item in the tariff or modifying the budget of the country you could solve the problem in one day, although I think we have been most unwise, the majority of this parliament, in approving of budgets rising to such heights as we have had in the last five years. But I do say the condition of trade and industry is the cause for unemployment in this country, and therefore the responsibility is on the government which is responsible for trade and industry.

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Rinfret
I say further that in Montreal, as in all large cities, the unemployed are not all from that city itself; they come from all over the province and even all over the country. I remember that when I was mayor of Montreal we had to deal with men who were sent to us by the mayor of Winnipeg. I merely mention that in passing as an illustration of the fact that when unemployment becomes general it is no longer a municipal or a provincial matter. There are certain centres in the country which are flooded with unemployed coming from all parts of the country, and it would be most unfair for the central government not to acknowledge its primary responsibility for dealing with that problem. I might point out also that with regard to a large city such as Montreal-and this would apply to Toronto or even to Sherbrooke-we do not receive the full benefit of all the money collected in the city. The harbour, the customs and the post office all collect money, in the main from activities taking place within the city limits, but that money belongs-and rightly so-to the central government. The central government has the power of taxation; it is able to call on many resources; it is able to exact money from those who should contribute it to the treasury of the country, but these opportunities are not open to the municipalities. Look at the difficulties with which the present administration in Montreal are faced. They have tried the income tax, the sales tax, this tax and that tax, but everywhere they are met with the condition which demonstrates that a problem such as this cannot be properly dealt with by only a small portion of the country. They want to tax a certain class of people in Montreal in order to meet the needs of the unemployed, but those people need only move to the next municipality in order to escape that tax, It is only the central power that can go to all the people of Canada and secure, through taxation or otherwise, the money needed for unemployment relief, and use it for that purpose.
Therefore I do say, Mr. Speaker, that if this responsibility has to be placed somewhere it should rest with the federal government. Yet, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, this government are not showing any signs of activity which would indicate that they are alive to their responsibility. On the contrary they seem to think that because they have provided a reform program which smacks very much of electoral disquiet, they have provided for the future, and that the present problems can be solved by leaving them alone or leaving them to be dealt with by local authorities. I remember that at the beginning of the session
there was some discussion as to the number of unemployed in the country. Statistics are very deceiving; if you consider the heads of families, their dependents, this class or that class you may suit them to your purpose, but I have in my hand a return brought down by the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) which places the number of persons on direct relief at 1,182,123. Those are the figures supplied by the government, and I do not think they show any decrease in the number of unemployed such as the Prime Minister attempted to point out in a former debate. On the contrary I think it is amply proven that there are vast numbers of people still on direct relief, and I say that unless the government have some policy to substitute for it the time is very ill chosen for any minister to announce to the country that the government are not going to pay their share and accept their responsibility in connection with direct relief, but are going to leave it to the provinces and the municipalities, contenting themselves with the payment of a lump sum.
I know, as everyone knows, that direct relief is an evil, but it has been rendered necessary because of the conditions that have arisen in the country. I repeat, however, and I think this is a fair statement to make, that direct relief is inevitable unless you have something else. It is all right to say that direct relief is not moral or that it is anti-social or something else, but if you do not provide work or if you have not a policy to deal with the problem in some more effective way are you going to let the people starve in order to show them that they are living in an unmoral state or something like that? Inasmuch as we must have it then I say the federal government should pay even a larger share than one-third of the cost of direct relief. If this government should drop out direct relief in Montreal would be left either to the province or to the municipality, and if that happened a condition would arise upon which I do not wish to dwell. In Montreal there are 225,000 people who depend upon the municipal cheque for their living. Do you imagine for a moment that you can turn those people loose and say there will be no cheque this week or next week? That would be a terrible state of affairs. It would be a new order of things, but not the new order that was promised in the Prime Minister's radio speeches. When the government say they are not going to pay more than a certain amount they practically accept the possibility of such a situation arising, and it is only because the government of the province and the administration of the city are more alive to their responsibility that this
1218	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Rinfret
condition does not come about. But that does not relieve this government of their responsibility through accepting, even in theory, a situation of that kind.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say that this amendment is very opportune, because it places the situation squarely before the country. Even if we are willing to accept the principle of unemployment insurance for coming years, together with the other reforms that have been announced-which have been in the programs of all parties, in fact, and have reached their place in the program of the present government only after being supported by the other parties in this country-we insist that the first thing we should have is a clear enunciation of policy by this government as to what they intend to do in regard to unemployment, because I say the disease of to-day is of much graver moment than the possible disease of five years hence. The reforms may be good in principle and even in practice, but they fail to touch that essential point. On the contrary the amendment brings that forward and reminds the country of the primary fact that the first thing to which this parliament should devote its attention, is the cure of our present evils and the certainty that these difficulties will receive consideration on the part of the government.
In conclusion may I say that I have no hope that the house will aocept the amendment. It is only natural to expect that hon. gentlemen opposite will vote against it. Though the Prime Minister claimed some weeks ago that we were now the Conservatives and that hon. gentlemen opposite had become the Liberals, I am afraid they have not become Liberal enough to vote for the amendment. It is my impression, from the way this session has been conducted, that the government did not expect that we on this side of the house would agree with their reforms. It was rather expected that we would oppose them from the very first, and perhaps force an election. Evidently the Prime Minister has been surprised by our attitude; in fact at times I think he has been surprised at his own. He is now somewhat embarrassed as to what he is to do next. I am giving him this advice in all good faith: Let him look first to the problem of unemployment because it is the most urgent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion now under discussion has to do with the most important problem which can come before parliament, and today the people of Canada are paying for forty years' neglect of it. This afternoon we heard from the representative of the

constituency of St. James (Mr. Rinfret), Montreal, and a former mayor of that city. The constituency of St. James is the home of the so-called capitalist system of Canada, which more than any other agency is to blame for the present unemployment situation.
It would be just as unfair for me to blame the former mayor of Montreal for the condition of affairs prevailing in that city, for the unemployment, the untold privation and suffering as it was for the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), assisted by the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Gray) to blame the government of Canada for the unemployment situation in the dominion.
May I observe in passing that the very same speech was made in Toronto by one of the hon. members who has spoken, and upon that occasion he complained that the Conservative government had not solved the unemployment condition in three days. Well, the hon. member for St. James was a part of the administration which held office from 1921 until 1930. That government was in office 5,697 days and did nothing but make a political football of the unemployment problem. The result was that when the present administration took office they found no organized plan either with the provinces or the municipalities which would have been sufficient to cope with the difficulty.
I am sorry to note the political trend of the discussion on this motion, because if there is one problem which should not be considered from a standpoint of party politics it is this particular problem which affects such large numbers of the men and women in the industrial centres in which such conditions have never before prevailed. I hope we will never again see the conditions under which many people who have been born in our cities and others who are new arrivals are living. They are enduring untold suffering, awful privations exceeding anything the human imagination can conceive, and this condition applies to skilled workers and other men and women who never knew what it was to lack a day's employment. These are most distressing conditions.
I am sorry to note the partisan stand taken by the Liberal party in connection with this proiblem. I admire the nature of the real liberalism which inspired the miners of Cornwall to march to London town to defend Bishop Trelawney against the tyranny of James II, as I do the freeholders of Buckinghamshire who defended John Hampden

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Church
against the tyranny of Charles Stuart. I cannot, however, admire the economic liberalism of the Liberal party in Canada, because I believe that economic liberalism, the policy adopted by those of the Manchester school and by those who for many years have been crying out for free trade and semi-free trade must bear some of the burden of blame for the condition of unemployment we have.
In my view the present economic problems of Canada cannot be solved by majorities in parliament. They must be dealt with by the nation as a whole, and as a matter of life and death. Our problems demand national sacrifice, and not parliamentary repartee, such as was attempted last night by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie). A remedy must be found for this great disaster of unemployment because it is the greatest disaster this or any other nation has ever experienced. The remedy must be as far reaching and uncompromising as the application of conscription was found to be in war. We have a war in Canada to-day, a war between thousands of our citizens on one hand and poverty and starvation on the other. Do not run away with the idea that the economic war is not as bad as a military war, because unemployment is as dangerous as a foreign foe in war time. Against a foreign foe we are united to repel invasion, but against our internal foe of unemployment we are not united and up to 1930 did nothing to check the advance of this enemy. In a time of military contest our country's resources are mobilized, and we have control of the transportation services, the man power and capital resources of the country. Under those circumstances we would be prepared and united to meet a foe, but when we have to meet a foe just as bad, namely the foe of unemployment, we are divided into political parties. Instead of standing united to solve this problem we are not united.
I believe our Prime Minister and the present government deserve a great deal of credit. I do not know where a great many of the municipalities would have been had it not been for the service given by the government now in office, because the government which preceded us for nearly nine years did nothing but make a political football of the whole problem. I mentioned between 1921 to 1930 the matter of unemployment on many occasions. May I say in passing that I would advise the hon. member for West Lambton who seconded the motion and is a past-president of the Sarnia senior rugby team dominion champions, to sign the hon.
member for St. James and the members of the cabinet of the former administration as members of his team next year on account of the football they made of unemployment from 1921 to 1930.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre made reference to two paragraphs in the speech from the throne. I have looked through the speeches from the throne for many years, and as a result I am led to make these observations. In the year 1926 I complained about the unemployment situation. At page 91 of the debates for that year I am reported as follows:
I very much regret that in the speech from the throne the government has given no indication that they are going to take any active steps to solve the economic ills of the country. There is the problem, for instance, of unemployment. Unemployment to-day in the larger centres of population is very acute. I might refer to the unemployment in the large manufacturing city from which I come. I know the conditions there, and I know that in the past three or four days very rapid preparations have been made by the social and charitable institutions and the public bodies of various kinds in the city to try and cope with the unemployment situation with which we shall he faced this coming winter.
We find nothing about unemployment in the speech from the throne of that year or for many years in which the previous government held office. The government which took office in 1921 had before it a report on unemployment ordered by the Union government in 1919 under Mr. Justice Mathers of Winnipeg. This report came as a result ol a national industrial conference which sat under Mr. Justice Mathers of Winnipeg. They travelled across Canada hearing evidence from public, commercial and manufacturing bodies. Later they made a report to the government in the fall of 1921, stating:
We recommended to your government-
The Union government-
-the question of making some provision by a system of state social insurance for those who through no fault of their own are unable to work, whether the inability arises from lack of opportunity, sickness, invalidity or old age. Such insurance would remove the spectre of fear which now haunts the wage earner and make him a more contented and better citizen.
Last night the hon. member for Vancouver Centre urged, as one of his nine points, the calling of another conference. By the time the Liberal party have another conference instead of being in the house of industry the unemployed will be dead and gone. By the time the Liberal party have another conference the unemployed will be dead and in

1220	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Church
the cemetery. My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) proposed a dominion-provincial conference to consider the question of financial relations between the provinces and the dominion, and secondly to consider unemployment, Canada's most urgent problem. The late Liberal government were nine years in power and had a report before them recommending sickness and unemployment insurance, and yet they did nothing to give effect to it. I myself brought this matter to the attention of parliament on many occasions in the nine years the Liberals were in power, and motions were also moved by my hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). I was a member of the committee on industrial and international relations for many years, and I supported this particular policy from the time that I entered the house till I left it in 1930 and I continually brought the matter to the attention of the late government. As late as February 25, 1929, I had this question on the order paper:
1.	Has the government any plans for providing employment for the great body of the unemployed?
2.	If so, what are they and what action will be taken, and when?
Mr. Heenan:
1.	The question of unemployment is one for the provincial governments.
2.	Answered by No. 1.
That was all they thought of it. That was the government of which my hon. friend from St. James (Mr. Rinfret) was a member. On March 5, 1930, I asked the government this question respecting unemployment relief:
1.	Has the government any plans for providing useful employment for the great body of the unemployed?
2.	If so, what relief will be afforded?
3.	Will the government accept the offer of the province of Ontario to provide one-third of the cost of certain forms of relief in conjunction with the federal and municipal authority; if not, why not?
Instead of answering that question the Liberal government asked to have it ruled out of order. I asked another question on March 13, 1930, with reference to an advisory economic committee. This was my question:
Will the government consider the appointment of an advisory economic committee for Canada to deal with economic questions?
The reply of the then Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was this:
This and kindred subjects are receiving the attention of the government.
In 1927 my hon. friend from Winnipeg moved a resolution in the house, and asked to have it referred to the industrial and international relations committee. That motion

was talked out of the house. By whom? It was talked out of the house on two occasions, in 1927 and again in 1928, by members who were supporting the government of that day. They prevented the hon. gentleman from having his case considered by the industrial and international relations committee at that time. It was just about that time that I presented the following resolution, adopted in 1927 by the ministerial association of the country:
Your committee, after careful enquiry and conference, respectfully submits concrete proposals, designed to help in solving the problems of relief and unemployment.
Your committee is conscious that results will depend upon the birth and cultivation of a public conscience, which shall demand that standard' of living in which no worthy citizen or his or her dependents shall suffer from hunger or cold by the operation of economic or other conditions beyond his or their control. To secure this conscience demands tact, tenacity and widespread use of the pulpit, the press, the platform, and every other form of advocacy.
Your committee believes that this association must employ its strength and zeal with determination to obtain the defined objectives.
Unemployment is an unsolved but solvable problem. It results generally from the operation of forces beyond the direct control of the wage-earner, and constitutes a menace and challenge to every citizen.
Your committee believes unemployment contributes to the moral, mental and physical deterioration of our citizens, and involves immense annual economic losses. It permits thousands of children to exist cold, neglected, under-nourished, and exposed to the most serious afflictions affecting the human race; it robs womanhood and manhood of character, their sense of self-respect, and shadow's their life outlook with shame and despair; it demoralizes unfolding youth, begets beggars and' vagrants; it is so far reaching in its effect upon society that generations unborn wall reap the awful harvest which follows inevitably in its wake.
Your committee believes the burden of responsibility to be a joint one resting upon all citizens and in particular embracing the federal, provincial and civic administrations. It would appear that the federal government has not been impressed by the serious and accumulative consequences of unemployment upon the citizens of the dominion.
Right down to the day the Liberal government left office I cannot find that they did anything of a practical nature to solve the unemployment problem, or to give relief to the municipalities of Canada, or to pay the municipalities one-third of the cost of relief. The municipalities had to deal with the unemployment problem for several years before the present government came into office, and before they got the help of this government, which was the most worthy help that was ever given to them. I do not know where

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Church
the constituents of my hon. friend from St. James would have been had it not been for the help that this government gave in the matter of unemployment relief and for the great work done by the Prime Minister and his cabinet to solve this unemployment problem.
This question also came up in the House of Commons in the session of 1923 in connection with the combines act. One of the main causes of the unemployment we have to-day has been the gigantic mergers and trusts and combines in restraint of trade which flourished unmolested from 1921 down to 1930, when the Liberals were in power. During that debate I proposed to write into the criminal code of this country the Sherman anti-trust law, and I proposed the appointment of a federal trade commissioner for Canada to regulate those abuses. I also proposed to add a section to the criminal code to give the grand jury at the assizes power to do the very work which a committee of this House of Commons has been doing for the past fifteen months, but that matter was not even considered by the government. I brought it up on many other occasions but it was rejected. So we can see, Mr. Speaker, all that was done by the Liberal government for the unemployed.
Another cause of unemployment has been the policy of economic liberalism in this country. Away back in the session of 1923, on the nineteenth of March, I moved a resolution in the house on Canada's coal supply, urging that we should have a national fuel policy for the people of this country so that we would not be left dependent on the United States. That resolution urged that the government immediately consider an allBritish and Canadian coal supply for Canada, whether the coal came from Wales, the maritimes or Alberta. When I proposed in this house a system of bonuses and subventions and subsidies for coal and grain and steel and iron, what was the policy of the government of which the hon. member for St. James was a member? It was to oppose the policy which I advocated, and not once but three or four years. Where would the maritimes have been to-day if it had not been for the policy which the Conservative party adopted under the leadership of the present Prime Minister? He is leading a party of reform, a party of real liberalism as we had it in England a hundred years ago at the time of the industrial revolution. Where would the maritimes have been had it not been for the assistance which the
92582-78 J
leader of this government gave them following out the policy advocated in my resolution which on many occasions hon. gentlemen opposite voted down? As a result of that policy the coal and steel and iron industries, which were withering industries in the maritimes, are to-day progressive and on the road to recovery.
What about grain? Agriculture, coal, and steel and iron are the three great key industries in this country, and the Conservative party has always been a consistent protectionist party with respect to them. The Conservative party under the leadership of the Prime Minister believes in giving protection to our own industries and in eliminating the abuses in the capitalist system. The basis of our policy has always been protection for two great classes in this country, agriculture and the industrial workers. Our policy has been our own work for our own workmen, and our own markets for our own' products. That is what made Canada a great industrial country, the country it is to-day. And where was the Liberal party in regard to this problem in the prairies? Where was the Hon. Mr. Crerar, who came down to my riding, a former Home bank director? Where were all these free traders? They were contending all along that the grain industry was a north and south industry, instead of an east and west industry, and they proposed free trade north and south. But we could not get any grain into the United States except our hard wheat. Afterwards there was an inquiry in the house and the then Prime Minister appointed Mr. Justice Turgeon of the Supreme Court of Saskatchewan to look into the question. Mr. Justice Turgeon found the very thing that I have pointed out; he said that there had been bootlegging of hard wheat in the elevators at Buffalo, Baltimore, New York and Boston. I was there and saw it myself. A great protectionist paper in Toronto, the Evening Telegram, spent thousands of dollars to prove its case, and it did prove it; and that is one of the reasons why the farmers of the prairies are in the condition in which they find themselves to-day. When the government of Sir William Hearst went out of power and the Drury government came in, Mr. Drury was not very long in office before he presented to the Prime Minister of this country in 1924 a resolution of the Canadian council of agriculture, and he denounced the manufacturers of Ontario and Quebec as thieves and robbers. The resolution complained that the farmers on the prairies had suffered from many unmitigated evils for many years, that the farmers
1222	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Church
had been exploited and plundered by those who enjoyed special privileges, and they requested to be relieved of the artificial barriers that stood in their way. Well, Ontario got rid of one of these obstacles in the form of the Drury government. Mr. Drury so denounced the manufacturers of Ontario that no manufacturer would invest any money in that province during the time that government was in office, with the result that industry got into a very bad state indeed. And where was Mr. Crerar all that time? I was never very enthusiastic about the Union government, but I will say this, that that goverment made a courageous effort in 1919 to rescue the farmers of the prairies, the people who were actually growing the grain, from these exploiters. As I said at that time, the greatest enemy of the man who grew grain in the prairies was not the manufacturer east of the great lakes but the big interests west of the great lakes, the grain combines and exchanges and elevator and transportation monopolies. Again I ask, where were these free traders when the grain industry was suffering in this way? We find that eventually they have had to come and ask this government to give them protection for this withering industry; they want a stabilization fund. But they were supporting free trade at that time. Mr. Crerar and his friends secured an injunction to prevent an investigation into the alleged system of robbery of the man who grows grain, but the Union government-and I give them credit for this-did try to do something practical for the farmers.
I have referred the house to two or three matters in connection with economic liberalisms, the economic liberalism of the Manchester school. I submit that the government of Canada might have done something practical regarding the St. Lawrence waterway. There was issued the other day a report to congress showing the magnificent success of the Panama canal. We know that they all laughed at Theodore Roosevelt when he put through that canal, but it is a magnificent success to-day, and no one knows how much it has contributed to employment the world over. If the government in 1921 had done something practical in connection with the St. Lawrence waterway, in conjunction with the United States, if they had pressed the matter year after year, we would have been prepared to meet the unemployment situation. Again, between 1921 and 1930 the question of a national hydro policy for this country came under consideration. What greater agency for the development of a country could there have been than that-a policy proposed right

in this house. We have 42,000,000 horse power in this country and only 7,000,000 developed, just one-sixth of all the potential water power capacity at our disposal. What was the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite when this matter was up, when the province of Ontario came here asking for a lead and proposed a federal policy for this country so that all power development power would be generated at cost and distributed to the two central provinces? The government of that day did nothing to put that policy into effect.
I say that we should all emulate the King in the calm words he used a year ago. There should foe calm words here instead of narrow partisanship. What did His Majesty say over the radio? His words were heard throughout the world on Christmas day a year ago, and I venture to say that if you canvassed the opinion of all reasonable men who heard him they would agree that we should reform our system. As the King said, we should have those qualities of unshakable sanity, invincible patience and tireless good will; those are the qualities we need to-day, which His Majesty so fittingly commended on that occasion. Hon. gentlemen opposite criticize the present government but I do not hesitate to say that this government did more in three months after coming into power, they did more for the unemployed in that time, than was done in the whole nine years the Liberal party was in office. This party has never been partial to the dole; the dole is only a temporary expedient, something which is intended to meet an emergency. As President Roosevelt said the other day, the lessons of history, confirmed by the evidence immediately before him, were conclusive on this point, that continued dependence upon relief tended towards moral disintegration and the fundamental destruction of moral fibre. As he said, the dole is a narcotic to the human spirit; it is inimical to the dictates of sound policy; it is a violation of the liberties of America. He urged work for every able bodied man and said that the federal government must quit the business of relief.
What did the Liberal party in this country do from 1921 to 1930? Owing to their complete failure to take any steps, the government which followed them in 1930 could do nothing but come to the aid of the struggling municipalities and assist them and the provinces, because many of the municipalities were facing bankruptcy. I do not know where the municipalities would have been had it not been for the aid that this government extended to them. It seems to me that the

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Church
Liberal party in Canada failed to realize the inroads which science had been making during the past nine or ten years into human labour; the machine has been the cause of unemployment everywhere. The machine is doing the work of man and man is not employed. All wealth was once created by the working classes and the soil combined; now it is created by the machine. The inventors, the rationalizers, the mass production experts, the clever fellows who have developed control over inanimate nature are making it more and more difficult for men to get employment. Judged by the old standard, the Canadian workmen's capacity to produce goods and services, the ordinary citizen would not be worth his salt; the machine can do the work better and more cheaply. But surely that is an absurd position for an industrial society to find itself in. For man first, last and always is the most important thing in civilization and a machine can produce everything but ideas.
We are living in a jobless age. Just the other day reference was made in the house to those of our population who were around eighteen years of age as living in a jobless age. What is going to be done with them I do not know7, but it is a problem regarding which I hope we shall get some constructive suggestions from hon. members opposite. I notice we did get one from the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) after hon. members on this side had made the very same proposals several years ago and again about a month ago in the house.
The question of unemployment insurance was brought up by the hon. member for North Winnipeg on March 16, 1927, and it was talked out at six o'clock by Liberal members. His motion was to refer the question to the committee on industrial and international relations. The question of unemployment insurance referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre last night was part and parcel of the Liberal platform, if you please, away back in 1919. Clause number 7 of this platform reads as follows:
That in so far as may be practicable, having regard to Canada's financial position, an adequate system of insurance against unemployment, sickness, dependence in old age, and other disability, which would include old age pensions, widows' pensions and maternity benefits, should be instituted by the federal government in conjunction with the governments of the several provinces; and that on matters pertaining to industrial and social legislation, an effort should be made to overcome any question of jurisdiction between the dominion and the provinces by effective cooperation between the several governments.
That was the platform of the Liberal party in 1919. They were elected to office on that in 1921, but although they remained in office for nine years they did nothing to put that platform into effect. Of course, as we know, a platform, as the late Hon. Israel J. Tarte said was made to get in on and not to stand on.
We have had visits from many hon. gentlemen opposite to my city, and in view of the partisan attitude taken by them in regard to this question I would like to refer to a brilliant book entitled The New Conservatism, written by Mr. W. S. Morrison, a British member of parliament, one of the most gifted of the younger Conservatives, and slated, as many British papers say, for very high office in Great Britain. He is criticizing the many-party system in his country. Speaking of Great Britain, he says:
The two old parties are done unless they open their ranks to new men and their minds to new ideas. There should be a modification of the present system or we will make a socialist government possible. The two old parties must be a constructive force for the building of a healthy social order based on economic and spiritual freedom or give place to those who have got an alternative program as an alternative to socialism. It is these conservatives that are the hope of the country.
These are the words of a great political leader of England, a young member of the British House of Commons and a man, as the London papers say, destined to high office in that country.
The municipalities are bearing a very heavy burden at the present time and this new legislation will be gladly welcomed by all classes of people. The industrial workers of this country are suffering as never before. As I said in the house the other day we need in parliament a type of member to bring to the attention of the house the anitiquated conditions of labour and of our maritime laws on the great lakes and their effect on unemployment and shipping. It seems more profitable for owners to lose vessels than to salvage them; our ship owners are protected by insurance. On the other hand in the fall of the year insurance for loss of life is practically nil in the upper lakes and because of this we have acute unemployment and many are suffering.
The dole is a help, but not a final remedy; it is only temporary. The policy of the Conservative party, notwithstanding statements made by hon. gentlemen opposite last night to the contrary, is not to place any more burdens or artificial barriers on business or trade and commerce or industry in this
1224	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Church
country, for to do so would not be modern protection. As our leader has said, I believe the new Conservative doctrine will be a greater aid to business, trade and commerce and industry generally than ever before, with protection brought up to date to take care of the consumer and labourer, to eliminate the abuses of the trusts, combines and mergers in restraint of trade which have borne so heavy a part in the unemployment of our people.
In the by-election in East Toronto we had a visit from many members of parliament from all over the country. The mover of the resolution, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, and many others were there. The issue raised in that riding was "Beat Bennett and bad times." As I said on that occasion, the present Prime Minister, the leader of the opposition when he was Prime Minister and the leader of the Progressive party had nothing to do with the condition into which the country had fallen; this was caused by world economic conditions brought about by the war and the disturbance of the industrial equilibrium. In that riding I paid tribute along that line not only to the head of the present government but to the other two hon. gentlemen to whom I have referred. I would be most unfair if I were to say of the Liberal leader what the hon. member for Vancouver Centre has said of ours, that he was responsible for conditions at that time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. SpeakeT, I desire to discuss briefly the amendment now before the house. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), in moving this resolution, brought forcibly before us the fact that the most urgent matter at present confronting the people of Canada is being sadly neglected by the present government. The resolution reads:
This house regrets that, notwithstanding the specific promises made prior to the elections of 1930, and many times since reiterated, and despite the fact that extraordinary powers to deal with unemployment have been repeatedly secured from parliament, the present administration, after nearly five years of office, has not yet submitted to parliament any definite or effective policy to deal with widespread actual unemployment or distress which continues to be Canada's most urgent national problem.
We are faced to-day with the most serious problem of unemployment that has ever confronted this country; we are faced too with a government that during the election campaign of 1930 promised the electorate that they had a formula for the cure of unemployment and that if they were returned to

power they would not only relieve the existing situation but absolutely cure it. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was most emphatic in his statements at that time; and some of the statements he made were put on Hansard last night by the hon. member who moved the resolution. He said he would cure unemployment or perish in the attempt. Now after a lapse of four and a half years we come back and are told by the right hon. gentleman who was leading the house last night (Sir George Perley) that we should not criticize the government, and we were told something the same this afternoon by the hon. member for East Essex (Mr. Morand). They say we should not criticize, that we should offer suggestions; but ever since the short session of 1930 we have been offering constructive suggestions to this government. If they look up the records of 1930 and every session since, they will see that not only my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) but others of this party have offered very constructive suggestions, which the government did not see fit to accept. Now, after a lapse of four and a half years this government must be judged by the results of the policies that they have put in force, and not by the promises that they are making for the future. The promises they made in 1930 that have not been fulfilled are still vividly in the minds of the people of Canada, and the government is to be judged by them rather than by the new array of promises that the Prime Minister broadcast at the new year.
In 1930, according to the records given at the short session of that year, there were
117,000	unemployed in Canada. That was just a little over the normal proportion of unemployment of the country. To-day we have over a million on relief. Not only has unemployment increased under this government, but trade has very materially decreased. In 1930 the total foreign trade of Canada, export and import, was over $2,000,000,000. In the last fiscal year it was down to $1,150,000,000 or thereabouts. It is further noticeable that the trade with the United Kingdom in 1930 was something over $474,000,000. We have heard a great deal about the benefits that the people of Canada got from the empire trade agreements, but in the last fiscal year the total trade with the United Kingdom was only about $343,000,000, or less by $130,000,000 than it was in 1930. In 1930 the sales tax was one per cent; at present it is six per cent, and

Unemployment Relief-Mr. McKenzie
not only that but this government have added practically all the nuisance taxes that we ever had during and following the war.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And sugar.
Mr. MoKENZIE (Assiniboia): Yes, sugaT, as my hon. friend reminds me. Then we hear a great deal to-day about our railway problem. No doubt it is a tremendous problem, but we did not hear much about it in 1930. 1 believe the main trouble with our railways to-day is lack of tonnage, largely a result of the policies of the present government. Not only is that true, but there is the condition of the farmers. In the part of the country from which I come they are practically bankrupt. I believe it is safe to say that seventy-five per cent of them are absolutely bankrupt, and another ten or fifteen per cent nearly so. It will be impossible for Canada to recover from the depression until more of our people are gainfully employed in useful occupations, and the obligation rests upon this government, which won the election of 1930 by promises to solve the unemployment problem, to bring in measures that will bring about that employment.
Last night the right hon. leader of the house told us that Canada was recovering from the depression faster than other countries. Coming from western Canada I cannot see much to be elated over or to be optimistic about in regard to recovery. I believe that any improvement there is in Canada is largely reflected from the N.R.A. in the United States. Instead of finding fault with us for our criticism of the government's policies the people of the country are wondering why the opposition have been so silent regarding the policies introduced this session. It is true that some social legislation has been introduced, but it has been disappointing in comparison with what the people were led to expect after hearing the Prime Minister in his broadcast on January 2 and on three or four subsequent occasions. So far as I can learn the part of the country that I represent can receive no benefit whatsoever from the unemployment bill. The other day I asked the Prime Minister whether or not the coal miners in my part of the country could benefit under it. He rather evaded the question; he did not give a very definite answer, but from what I could gather there is no hope whatever of those men receiving any benefit from this legislation, and of course the farming community cannot benefit.
This country has been going from bad to worse for the last four or five years as far as employment is concerned. We began to take the toboggan immediately after the high tariff legislation introduced at the special session in 1930. It may be true that there has been a slight improvement during the past few months. This government introduced their "Canada first" policy in 1930 and tried to make Canada self sustained. Now if there is one country in the world that we look upon as largely capable of being self contained it is the United States, but even the United States has to import a considerable number of products, for instance nickel, and pulpwood, and other products which they must obtain in Canada. They also must import rubber. Great Britain must import at least two-thirds of her foodstuffs; France has to import oil. Every civilized country has to import some product; it is impossible for even the older nations of the world to be self contained. Therefore it was utter folly to think of Canada becoming a self contained nation. This government's policies have now been in operation for over four years, and it has been established beyond doubt that their theories and formulas for the improvement of the situation have failed and are of no avail. I have always been at a loss to understand why this government took the attitude they did, particularly following the short session of 1930. The Prime Minister seemed to think that all he had to do was to increase the tariff and the unemployment situation would be relieved and prosperity would return. But after he saw the effect of that policy I cannot understand why the government continued it. In 1930, when business collapsed and wages and salaries went down, the prices of commodities would have declined also had it not been for the high tariff policy of the government. I do not understand how the government ever thought it would be possible for the labouring men of this country, who received very moderate salaries and who, owing to the policies of this administration, had their wages reduced-because high tariffs and low wages go hand in hand-to continue to pay for what they had to buy, their clothing, their food and other requirements, at the old prices. Not only that, but if the labouring man was a taxpayer his taxes were greatly increased. The situation of the farmers was even worse; their incomes were reduced in many cases by as much as seventy-
1226	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. McKenzie
five per cent, but still they were expected to pay the same prices for everything they had to buy, as well as increased taxes.
I remember that in 1931 the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), who was fresh from the province of Saskatchewan and who knew the feeling of the farmers of that province with regard to high tariffs, introduced a measure providing for a bonus on wheat, and said that it was a compensating adjustment to the farmers of western Canada in view of the high tariffs that had been raised. I have been waiting to hear what the minister is going to introduce now as a compensating adjustment to the farmers of the west not only because of the high tariffs but also because of the extra taxes they will have to pay for the administration of this unemployment insurance measure. The farmers cannot benefit from that measure any more than they can benefit from high tariffs; it is impossible for the farmers to benefit from either.
It seems to me the government are very lax in regard to measures to relieve the unemployment situation. There is nothing in the legislation that has been brought down, including the unemployment insurance bill, to relieve the present unemployment situation. In addition there are many other challenges presenting themselves to the government. with which the government are not grappling. In the first place there is the interest on our bonded indebtedness. Some few years ago, after the government had negotiated a loan of some $200,000,000 at five per cent interest, I said that I believed they could have borrowed that money for at least one per cent less, which would have meant a considerable saving in the annual interest. This interest on our bonded indebtedness makes a very considerable levy on our income each year, and the problem must be dealt with sooner or later. In addition we have another problem facing us; I refer to the pension indebtedness of the country. 1 have often asked myself why every person working for the government should be entitled to a pension. Sooner or later this pension business will have to be dealt with. I believe we are overdoing it. It is a good thing, but you can easily overdo a good thing, and I believe our pension schemes have been entirely overdone. There is also another matter which I believe must be dealt with; I refer to over-employment in our civil service. I have received quite a number of letters from people in my constituency complaining that there are too many people being employed by the government in the higher 
salaried classes. I think it is true; I believe there are altogether too many civil servants receiving exorbitant salaries.
The unemployment situation is the most serious problem confronting us, but there is another great problem which should be considered by the government and which has not been dealt with by any of the legislation that has been brought down. That question is how our farmers are to survive the present depression. They cannot survive unless something is done, by reducing interest and in other ways, in order to help them. It cannot be done by increasing their taxes through the introduction of such measures as the unemployment insurance bill, which the Prime Minister told us would mean the addition of four thousand employees to the civil service. The farmers are going to ask just what they will receive from this legislation, and I ask the government before this session is finished to endeavour to devise some scheme whereby the farmers can be kept on the land and helped through the present depression.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.
