speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, February 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Reid for the second reading of Bill No. 17, to amend the Fisheries Act, 1932.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations on the second reading of Bill No. 17. First may I say I believe it would have been better had this matter been brought before the house by way of resolution. Probably that action would not have been quite so spectacular from a political standpoint, but I believe it would have been just as effective, perhaps more so, than the method which has been adopted of bringing it to the attention of hon. members. I do not believe it was ever intended that parliament should replace regulations by legislation in matters of administration under the control of the departments. If we are to undertake to adjust by legislation every grievance in every corner of this great country, then we must be prepared to sit here twelve months of the year not only to pass legislation but to amend it.
Let me point out the danger in the present instance. So far as I am concerned, if the bill receives second reading, well and good. In that event the principle would be adopted, and seining would be prohibited in district

Fisheries Act
No. 1, British Columbia. If the bill is defeated on second reading, then the matter is closed. I doubt very much whether all hon. members from British Columbia will support the bill, but even if they did. a majority of the house may not see fit to interfere with the regulations as applied to certain fishing districts on the Pacific coast. That is a matter which in my view should rest entirely in the hands of the minister and the government. Under the act the parliament of Canada has given powers of regulation. Nevertheless I welcome this opportunity to discuss this matter and to bring directly to the attention of the minister and the government certain conditions pertaining to seine fishing at the mouth of the Fraser river.
The constituency I have the honour to represent is perhaps not so much concerned in this matter as the districts lying directly west. While in my constituency there are hundreds depending on the industry, other constituencies number their dependents by thousands. In the Fraser Valley constituency there are, however, a large number of good citizens located along the Friser river who for a number of years have followed the occupation of gill net fishing. Throughout those years they have been able to make a comfortable living for themselves and their families. In the last couple of years they have found their incomes greatly curtailed, in some instances to such an extent that municipalities have represented to me and to other hon. members that in the past year some of the families of these men have had to accept relief.
I have discussed the matter with representatives of the gill net fishermen, and they have protested strongly against the department permitting seine fishing in district No. 1. Their submission is that seine fishing is most destructive and will eventually destroy the established industry of gill net fishing on the Fraser river. I have discussed the matter not only with the representatives of the fishermen but with the Department of Fisheries, and I believe it would be only fair to the department to place on record the main reasons given for the introduction of seining in this particular district. I have before me a memorandum prepared by the department, and I shall quote that portion which presents their side of the case, following which I shall undertake to place on record the facts presented by the fishermen.
The first point presented by the department is as follows:
The main runs of the different species of salmon to the Fraser make their way to Canadian waters through Juan de Fuea strait and the lower portion of the gulf of Georgia that is within United States waters, During that time by far the largest portion of the catches that are made on both sides of the line is effected in the United States waters with purse seines and trap nets.
The argument there is that we should get in and catch some of the fish now being taken by the Americans. The fishermen point out that apparently the Americans have seen the error of their ways in the using of traps, and have taken them out. There is also the possibility of the Americans prohibiting seining. Even the continued use of seines in American waters is not a good argument for the use of seines in Canadian waters. I am advised there is no comparison between seining at the mouth of the Fraser river and seining on the American side of the line. On the American side, the fish travelling more or less rapidly towards the mouth of the Fraser river, about two hundred seine boats are scattered over a distance approximately of two hundred miles whereas on the Canadian side of the line over one hundred seine boats are operating over a distance of less than ten miles. As the regulations stand there is nothing to prevent another hundred boats moving in, whenever they wish. It is a well known fact that as the sockeye cross the Canadian border the water becomes more brackish, and the fish on entering fresh water have a tendency to slow down, to play around and to gather in schools in preparation for entering the river. This is where the seines get in their deadly work and where the slaughter is wholesale. To show just how-deadly seine fishing can be, my attention was drawn to a report of one week's seining allowed by, the department in district No. 1 during the first week of September, 1934. The report showed that the last day's catch of the week was only ten per cent of the first day's catch,, indicating that all the fish had been caught. That deals with the question so far as the competition with the American fishermen is concerned.
The main argument lodged by the department has to do with quality. I have before me the particular portion of the memorandum dealing wTith that point; it reads as follows:
While tile pink salmon are in first class condition all the time they are in United States waters, and while as a consequence vastly larger quantities of them have been packed there than has been the case on the Canadian side, unfortunately for us we are faced with the fact that by the time these fish reach the
Fisheries Act

Fraser river waters they are so nearly approaching spawning condition that their quality has fallen off, and it continues to deteriorate so much that it is only the earlier fish that will make a creditable pack. Since inspection of canned salmon became a factor, there is much less readiness to pack poor quality goods than was previously the case. Consequently if fishing for pinks were restricted on our side to gill netting, gill net catches would be bound to be small owing to the lack of demand for the fish.
Then further, referring to the late run of sookeye:
Since 1926 there has been coming to the Fraser in quite large quantities what are commonly called late run soekeye. These have been occurring two years out of the four year cycle; that is, 1926 and 1927, again in 1930 and 1931, and again in 1934 and 1935. These fish, like the pinks, while of good quality when they are in the United States waters, are definitely off quality when they begin to ascend the Fraser, so if purse seining for them were not permitted and inspection maintained, as with the pinks, there would be little demand for them from the gill netters.
1 should like to refer to the first paragraph I quoted in regard to quality. It says that the pink salmon are so nearly approaching spawning condition by the time they reach the Fraser river that their quality has fallen off. Those of us who live on the Fraser river know that the spawning grounds are from fifty to sixty or seventy-five miles, and perhaps further than that, from the mouth of the Fraser. We are also told by those who are in a position to judge that these fish feed while in salt water, and that they cease to feed as soon as they enter the fresh water, and that is the time that the fish is in a better condition.
As to quality, the gill net fishermen point out that the pink salmon, whether taken by seine or gill net, are oaught in practically the same waters, the boats even operating side by side, and if there is any difference in< the quality it should be in favour of the gill net caught fish as there is a vast difference in the handling oif the catch en route to the- canneries. The gill net fish are collected in small boats, the loads rarely exceeding three thousand fish, while the seine boats carry a load of from 20.000 to 30,000 fish, and these fish are dropped from the brail, a distance of from twelve to fifteen feet. Naturally, with a soft fish like the pink salmon, the weight of this load, approximately seventy-five tons, when packed into a wedge shaped hull leaves the bottom fish in a mess that has to be seen to be appreciated. Often five thousand or more of the fish at the bottom of the boat have to be thrown overboard, and there is no doubt that a certain percentage of the

others are not in prime condition. Undoubtedly the fish caught and handled in this manner must account for a considerable proportion of the so-called inferior grade. But that is the system by which this oountry,. apparently, through the ruling of the department, is endeavouring to obtain a higher grade product.
These men claim that the late run of sock-eye and pink salmon might be caught while they are in better condition if there were a longer weekly closed season and the fish were permitted to enter the river while in prime condition. The high quality of the pack would then be maintained without the use of seines.
Hon. gentlemen may have noticed that reference was made in the first paragraph of the memorandum from which I have quoted to gill net fishermen being unable to supply the fish in quantity. The gill net fishermen have made application year after year to increase the length of their nets 150 to 200 fathoms in order that they might increase the size of their catch.
On the question of quality, we have as evidence, that the gill net fish are of a higher quality in the fact that last year the gill net fishermen received sixty cents for their fish while the seiners received fifty cents.
It has been represented by certain interests that the trouble in this district No. 1 is between two classes of fishermen. That is not the case. The trouble is between the interests that own practically all the seine boats and equipment, and the fishermen; and I wish to point out that the interests that own the seine boats and equipment require five-twelfths of the catch to be handed over to them in lieu of their investment. But these big interests are not the only ones that have a heavy investment in the fishing industry. The gill net fishermen also have a very large investment, and that brings me to the claim which these men make that many misleading figures have been published by the department regarding their income, their investment, and the number of boats engaged in the gill net fishing industry. Apparently this information has been secured from the canning and packing industry. The figures issued by the department show an investment by the gill net fishermen of some $800,000, while the fishermen themselves claim that their investment is closer to $2,000,000. The number of boats estimated by the department engaged in gill net fishing is 1,600, which the men claim is an error; they state that during the last

Fisheries Act
soekeye season no less than 3,500 gill net boats were engaged in fishing in district No. 1.
It would appear to me that the question to be considered is this: Is it in the best interests of this country to continue to curtail the income of thousands of our citizens in order to satisfy the claim made by the department that a better grade of fish is being secured through seine fishing than through gill net fishing? I would say that no satisfactory evidence has been produced in support of that claim. My own opinion and it is based on information which I have secured from the men and from the department, is that it would be wise to prohibit seining for the next two years in order to check up on this question of quality. Oh, yes, the department tell us that they have no intention of permitting seining next year, the reason being that there will be no fish. But this is the year of the big run, and that is one reason why I think that the minister and the government in view of conditions should consider seriously throwing it open to the gill net fishermen and give them the advantage in this year of the big run.
I am quite willing to leave this matter to the judgment of the minister. I suggest to him that if he has not satisfactory evidence before him to justify making this change and cancelling the present regulation, he appoint someone perhaps outside the department, someone who is not interested in the canning or packing business, to go out into that district and go right out on the land or on the water and investigate and secure any information which the minister might require in order to deal with this matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish to say a few words in support of Bill No. 17 introduced by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). To me this is the age old question, as old at least as capitalism itself, of hand production versus machine production. Gill net fishing is a form of hand fishing and purse seine fishing is a form of large scale production. There are two questions which the government should keep in mind: first of all, the preservation of the fish in the fishing areas so that there may be supplies of fish so long as there are any human beings in need of them; and secondly, the welfare of all those engaged in the fishing industry. The fishing industry should be considered as a means of livelihood for the people in the surrounding country. If more people can secure a livelihood by the use of the seine, then that would be the proper method to follow. But
it seems to me it has been proved that this is not so; it has been proved that seine fishing deprives a great number of fishermen of their livelihood while it gives a greater advantage to a small number of canners. That being so, I think the position of the minister is rather an easy one, regardless of what may have been done in the department before he came into office. He is now the minister and he is not bound by what took place before he took that office.
I do not know whether it would have been better to bring this matter before the house by way of a resolution rather than in the form of a bill, but I do not think it makes much difference. If the government would have accepted a resolution there is no reason why they cannot accept the bill. I was not here when the matter was discussed, but I understand that the hon. member introducing it asked that it be referred to the fisheries committee. I hope that the minister will see his way clear to refer it to that committee, and that when that is done an opportunity will be given some of the representatives of the gill net fishermen to appeaT before the committee. I attended a meeting in 'New Westminster early in the winter when the deputy minister, Doctor Found, was present, and I am sure that anyone who was at that meeting must have been struck with the intense feeling of the gill net fishermen. They had a feeling that they were being done out of their livelihood by the use of seines. I appeal to the minister to allow the bill to go to the committee on fisheries. I am pleased at the reasonable attitude adopted by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber), and I add my word to his in an appeal to the minister to have the bill referred to the fisheries committee, where it may be discussed on its merits.

speakeroldname: Hon. GROTE STIRLING (Acting Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member who sponsors this bill (Mr. Reid) proposes to prohibit the catching of salmon by the use of purse seines. This is a controversial matter which has been before the house on previous occasions, but no one has ever attempted to deal with it by inserting in the Fisheries Act an amendment which would prohibit the use of purse seines. When I was out on the Pacific coast early in December I had the privilege of meeting delegations from the gill netters, from the purse seine men and from the canners. On the latter occasion only passing reference was made to this question. The hon. member who sponsors this bill was present when I met the gill netters. In his statement before the house on the second
Fisheiies Act

reading he, in my opinion, stated but one side of the question; and because he omitted several points which I think are salient, I propose to devote a few minutes to placing those points before the house.
Prior to 1916 the taking of salmon in these waters which we are discussing was prohibited after August 25, and the reason therefor was that the fish towards the end of the main run were not in prime condition for canning purposes after that date. They enter the straits of Juan de Fuca and hug the Washington coast, and are taken there by the United States fishermen in far greater quantities than they are on the Canadian side of the line running down the centre of those straits. As the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) has said, until recently they have been taken in fish traps by United States fishermen, and by purse seiners as well. The fish traps have now been prohibited, and whether that prohibition will continue or not time only will tell. But intruded into this question of recent years has been the extensive runs of late sockeye. These fish come around on the Washington coast, and it is not until they enter the Canadian waters along the line running close to Boundary Bay, which is not so many miles south of the mouth of the Fraser river, that they can be taken by Canadian fishermen. The gill netters fish in the Fraser river and in the discoloured waters of the gulf of Georgia adjacent to the mouth of it, and they confine their attention principally to these discoloured waters, because in the clearer waters of the gulf the drifting gill net is visible to the fish and the fish at least endeavour to avoid it. The consequence is that the gill netters are found principally in the discoloured waters at the mouth of the Fraser river, and if they do move on into the adjacent clear water they find that they are not taking fish in the same quantities, and so they get back into the discoloured water.
Now, after 1916 there was a general desire for an increase of food, and the fishing season was therefore extended to last from July 1 to October 31. The hon. member who sponsors this bill left on the house, I think, the impression that when the seiners began by regulation to fish, they fished in the same waters and presumably for the same length of time as did the gill netters. In 1934 the purse seiners were permitted to fish from September 1, but the gill netters had begun at the beginning of the season on July 1; and on September 8 fishing was stopped by the supervisor of fisheries for conservation reasons. As two of the days between the first and the eighth of September were two weekly days of

closing for conservation purposes, the seine fishers fished only for six days at the beginning of September. Conservation having been satisfied, fishing was again permitted on the first of October. So poor was the quality of the fish that the seiners fished for only two or two and a half days and then fishing ceased. Therefore the seiners were allowed by regulation to fish in the clear waters of the gulf, not infringing upon the discoloured waters in which the gill netters fish, for only a total of eight and a half days last fishing season, whereas the gill netters in the river and in the adjacent waters near the mouth were able to fish from July 1 until fishing was stopped except for the two days a week for conservation. I do not think the hon. member made that plain to the house.
With regard to the numbers that he claims are included in the rank of the gill netters, he states that 2,366 gill net fishermen are employed. I do not know the source of his figures, but they do not agree with those of the department and it must surely know the number of licences issued. The total number of fishermen was 1,705, of whom 1,266 were white; 39, Indians; 400, naturalized orientals, and 234, fishermen who had taken licences for other areas and had them later transferred to the Fraser. In addition to the above there were 335 assistants to the fishermen. Of these, 34 were whites, one was an Indian, and 300 were naturalized orientals, making a total of 2,040 instead of the 2,366 mentioned by my hon. friend. Those fishermen and their assistants are, I presume, residents on the banks of the Fraser river and naturally are particularly interested in the process of fishing known as gill net. The seiners on the other hand come from further afield. Last year there were 103 seine boats. As the crew varies in numbers from seven to eleven men, we may say that perhaps 900 would be an average of the crews of the boats. Besides that there were the carrying boats. We may say therefore that there were
1,000	seiners interested. Those seiners come from away up north, from Skeena, Comox-Alberni, the Vancouver district, and they are just as much interested in this question we are discussing as are the gill netters.
The position taken by the department in this controversy has been to endeavour to hold the balance even between these two methods of taking the fish. It became evident in 1930 and 1931 that consequent on the scramble for world markets, the Canadian canners were losing out in those markets owing to the extreme competition of United States and Japanese canneries in the matter

Fisheries Act
of quality. They could not get a sufficiency of the quality desirable for their first grade canning. The fish, as I have pointed out already, come up and enter the clear waters to the south of the discoloured water at the Fraser river. They apparently cannot toward the end of the season be taken in sufficient quantities to supply the needs of the Canadian canner and consequently by regulation restricted seining was permitted for a certain time. My hon. friend the sponsor of the bill in his earlier statement expressed the opinion that it was not possible for the canners to keep the seine caught fish and the gill net caught fish separate. My information is to the contrary; it is that at least some of the canners are at particular pains to keep the gill net fish separate from the seine fish and so are able to say what proportion of the gill net fish and similarly, what proportion of the seine caught fish are prime, firm in flesh, suitable for a high quality of canning. Their opinion is that toward the end of the season they can get the desired quantity from fish taken in the cold clear waters of the gulf and they are not able to get them from fish taken in the discoloured waters in the Fraser river.
My hon. friend also referred to the fact that regulations were passed by the department and fired at the gill net fishermen without notice. I do not think that is quite a fair statement of the case. Every fall the chief supervisor of fisheries invites from the industry recommendations based on the past season's fishing. Those are received; perhaps they are added to in the' form of recommendations by the chief supervisor himself; they are considered; they are tabulated and they are sent out to the fishermen's organizations. Those' organizations have an opportunity to express their opinions thereof and then the department takes the necessary steps to arrange what the regulations for the coming season shall be. An order in council is then passed, and obviously it is not possible before the order in council is passed to pass on to those organizations the definite wording of the regulations. When it is passed the fishermen's organizations are so informed. I do not see in what other way ' it would be possible to keep in touch with those organizations.
It is quite obvious to me that the only role that the Department of Fisheries can take in this matter is to endeavour to hold the balance even. The fish are there to be caught, and surely no one type of fishermen can have a prescriptive right to state what method shall be adopted in order to take the fish.
There was a great controversy before the regulations of 1932 were adopted. Every effort was made on the part of the department to try to draw those two sets of people together in order to arrive at a compromise which would satisfy both. When that was found to be impossible and the United States fishermen were taking fish by the millions while the Canadian fishermen were taking them in much smaller quantities, it was evident that something had to be done in order to enable this industry which we have been building up with such success to continue to fill the needs of the market.
My hon. friend suggests that the bill should be permitted to go to the fisheries committee. I cannot accept the principle of the bill, but with that proviso I have no reason to object to its going to the fisheries committee for further consideration and discussion. It must however not be taken that the government accepts the principle of this method of prohibiting the taking of salmon by seines in the waters referred to. My hon. friend has suggested that if the bill should go to the fisheries committee it would be desirable that these fishermen should come and give evidence before the committee. We must wait until the committee makes a recommendation with regard to that but it is quite obvious to me that both contesting parties must have the same opportunity and invitation to come and give their evidence. I very much question whether witnesses coming from that distance can add any new facts to those already collected on the subject, but as I say it is for the committee to state its wishes so far as witnesses are concerned. I do not object to the bill being submitted to the select standing committee on marine and fisheries so long as it is clearly understood that the government does not accept the principle laid down.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As the acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Stirling) has stated that he is willing that this matter be considered by the committee on marine and fisheries, my remarks will be very brief. I am disappointed that the minister makes the reservation that the government will not accept the principle of the bill. To me that is a straight direction to the committee in advance that the principle of prohibiting seines in that area does not meet with the approval of his department or of the government. I thought when he was going to refer the bill to the committee he would do so without any such reservation,
Fisheries Act

allowing the committee to decide the matter after hearing evidence, if they consider it necessary to call evidence.
In view of the fact that the acting minister has stated that in my address the first evening I presented only one side of the matter, let me point out that I have endeavoured to show both sides. I will state one fact to show how keen the cannery men are that only their side of the case shall be given to the minister, and nothing given to members of parliament or others who are interested. In 1931 I endeavoured to learn what the canners were doing, and, hearing that the Deputy Minister of Fisheries -was to meet them in Vancouver I made it my business to go there and sit in at the meeting. It was held on a Saturday afternoon. The room was full of cannery men. I asked the deputy minister if he had any objection to my sitting in, and he said no. But when I walked in to the meeting you should have seen the look of consternation on the faces of those canners. Their hair almost stood on end. I said: "Gentlemen, I might just as well tell you who I am. I happen to be the member for New Westminster representing the fishermen of the Fraser river, and I am interested in this industry. I have heard the fishermen s side and now I want to hear the canners' side." One canner got up and said: "Mr. Deputy Minister, I thought this was a private meeting." It became so embarrassing that they did not know what to do. One member said: "I suggest that Mr. Reid go out of the room until we discuss this question." I went out and took my hat and coat and went off; as a member of parliament I was not going to stand waiting like a flunkey outside the door of a canners' meeting. That is the trouble: the deputy minister goes out there and meets the canners and gets an earful from them, and they come to Ottawa and give him another earful and then he holds a meeting with the fishermen. But until such time as a deputation of the fishermen and a deputation of the canners meet together with him on common ground this matter will never be satisfactorily settled. I would welcome the bringing from the Pacific coast of representatives of the canners' interests as well as those of the fishermen. I think now is the time that the whole matter should be gone into.
I was very sorry to hear the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) say: "I am in favour of this but I do not like the way the hon. member introduced it." Next time perhaps I shall consult him first when I am going to introduce a bill. But, Mr. Speaker, the fact is that if I had introduced this by

way of resolution he and a few of his friends might have talked it out and to-day we would find it at the foot of the order paper and so it would never be heard from again. I knew their tricks and their manners, and I introduced it as I did so that it would come squarely before the government. I speak as I feel in this matter because the livelihood of over 2,000 fishermen is at stake; they are threatened with being driven out by the vested interests who control and own most of the seines. I deprecate the acting minister giving the direction to the committee that the government is not going to accept the principle of the bill. I urge on the members of the committee that all interested parties be brought before them so that this whole matter, in which not only the livelihood of the men but the whole salmon industry itself is at stake, shall be fully heard. I am quite willing, however, to accept the suggestion of the minister and leave my further remarks for the committee.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the select standing committee on marine and fisheries.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Rhodes for committee of supply and the amendment thereto of Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver Centre).

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: After listening for something over a month to the declarations of anxiety on the part of hon. members opposite that we should bring down our legislation and go forward with our reforms and get on with the business of the country, the icy blast that inundated this chamber last night from Vancouver came to us with something of a shock.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: You are thinking of Hudson bay.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: To my mind all this is nothing short of a crude and organized attempt to divert public attention from the real issue that confronts this house and the people of this country to-day. The reform program of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is the issue now before the house. I can quite understand our Liberal friends being a little worried-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Very little.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
For a year or two they were basking in the sunshine of a few

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Stitt (Nelson)
provincial victories, with the federal election already won, and they did not feel that they had to say or do very much. But the Prime Minister's program of reform gave them a great shock. I venture to say there will be a still greater shock coming to them when the smoke of the next election has cleared away. It is all right for them to damn the government and damn the Prime Minister and hon. members on this side for inactivity in regard to unemployment, but this was something that came to us as a legacy from the party opposite; it was left on our doorstep when we took over in 1930. It is true the leader of the government made certain promises then, and I believe he was sincere when he made them. But I do not think in 1930 any member of this house could have foreseen what was ahead of us. Most hon. members thought the depression was more or less a local affair that would blow over in a year or two, as other depressions had, and I think the right hon. leader of the government can be absolved from many of the promises he made at that time. I believe any fairminded man will admit that.
I think our friends opposite would be well advised to withhold their criticism until such time as the Prime Minister has brought down all his reforms. One or two measures have been brought down and proceeded with, but I want to tell hon. gentlemen that they have not heard half of it yet. They are ill advised to start throwing sand in the machinery at this time. I quite appreciate that hon. members may be carried away by some of the things they hear and see in these days of stress and strain, but let me say that they have no monopoly of sympathy for the unemployed, those poor unfortunates who through no fault of their own find themselves in a desperate condition. I think we on this side of the house have suffered as many sleepless nights as hon. members opposite, and we are just as sincere and just as much interested as they are in trying to find some remedy. We are looking for helpful suggestions, not for criticism. So far we have received mainly criticism from hon. gentlemen opposite, and destructive criticism at that. We have not been able to put through one piece of legislation in the last four years, no matter how helpful it may have been, without running up against almost a blockade from the other side of the house. Much of the legislation we said would be helpful, and it has turned out to be helpful. If hon. gentlemen are really sincere when they say they wish to assist this government to put through their program, why not climb on the
construction train instead of throwing obstructions on the track? It might be well for some hon. gentlemen opposite to remember that a hammer can be used to build up as well as to tear down.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) spoke with great gusto about world trade, and damned this government for high tariffs. He is not very consistent; it was not very long ago that he made a statement in this house which I should like to quote. Referring to page 4258 of Hansard for June 25, 1934, I find the hon. member quoted as follows:
I am in favour of reduced tariffs all over the world, but I recognize that it may be very difficult for us alone to reduce tariffs when all other nations are maintaining theirs.
Mr. Bennett: Good! At last!
Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver): We are discussing this in a very frank way.
The hon. member might be at least consistent when he speaks about tariffs. I should like to go a step further and quote another front bencher on the opposite side. This is an extract from a speech delivered on October 28, 1932, by the ex-Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler):
I have always felt, and still feel, perhaps in a sense more than ever when all the other nations of the world, or practically all, have erected impenetrable barriers against our products, that it is only fair that we should have such a tariff as will enable our own producers to have a fair chance in their own market.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Where is there any inconsistency in what I have said since?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
I have not said there was any inconsistency on the hon. member's part. I am simply quoting the statements of some of the front benchers opposite in order to show the inconsistency of the party as a whole.
Now I should like to say a word in regard to trade. One would almost think Canada was the only country in the world that suffered any loss of trade, but what are the facts? We will all cheerfully agree that Canada experienced colossal trade during some of the years hon. gentlemen opposite were sitting on this side of the house, but in 1928 and 1929, especially after the adoption of the Hawley-Smoot tariff in the United States, trade started to fall off. It was only natural that Canada, together with all the other exporting countries of the world, should suffer some decline in trade. The chief statistician of the League of Nations issued a statement showing that in 1929 the world trade amounted to 868,000,000,000, in round figures. In 1930 it had dropped to 855,000,000,000. In 1931 it
1234	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Stitt (Nelson)
was only 839,000,000,000 and in 1932 only $26,000,000,000, or about one-third the trade of 1929. What happened in Canada; did our trade decline by two-thirds? Our trade is about fifty or sixty per cent of what it was in the banner years when the Liberal government was in power. One year we did drop back from fifth to sixth place among the trading nations of the world, but now we are back in fifth position, which is not a bad record in view of the statement made by the statistician of the League of Nations.
I am not going quite so far as some hon. members on this side of the house have gone;
I do not say the Liberal party were responsible for the drop in trade or the loss of markets. I do not think they had any more to do with it than we did. The world became obsessed with mad, economic nationalism, and we were sliding down that slippery hill towards ruin and despair. The United States took the lead long before we fell in line; as a matter of fact that country set the pace for us, as was admitted by Mr. Cordell Hull, secretary of state for the United States. Not very long ago that gentleman said:
Extreme nationalism, if persisted in, is destined soon to wreck our entire structure of western civilization.
He stated that the United States started it and most of the other countries fell in line, so we were driven to any action we took in this country. For one or two years after the depression set in United States industries were bonused by the government; under their codes they voted billions of dollars to stiffen up industry and keep it going. As a result practically all the available warehouses were filled with goods, and they were anxious to dump them on any market at any price. If the Canadian government had not taken the action they did take in 1930 practically every factory in this country would have been closed up within sixty days. It must have been disconcerting to some of the Liberals to see the figures contained in an article on the front page of the Ottawa Citizen this morning. The headline reads:
Trade Figures Show Canada's Sharp Advance.
During 12 months ended January 31, her exports to world exceeded imports by $131,830,000.	.	.
24T per cent growth in Empire business.
Upturn of 20-9 per cent in commerce with foreign countries also revealed.
That does not sound very much like the stories some of our Liberal friends are telling, that we are strangling trade and losing what trade we have. We lost our trade for the same reason that every other country lost its trade; the world went crazy on economic

nationalism and purchasing power was destroyed. I am ready to admit that on the surface it would appear the Liberals have the wind behind them. We must remember that in the last three or four years they have been doing most of the talking. The conservative party and its great leader, Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, have been too busy to answer the tradueers of Canada; we have been trying to save this ship of state from destruction. But from now on we will go out -on the hustings and tell the people our side of the story; we will give them the true picture of conditions which existed when we came into office; we will explain what has been done since and the courageous steps we have taken to meet those conditions.
I do not know why it is necessary for hon. members opposite to rise day after day and damn the leader of this party and his followers. In passing may I say to hon. members opposite that hon. members on this side of the house have yet to see our leader, in whom we have every confidence and for whom we have the greatest respect, rise in his place in this chamber and tell the people of Canada that he and his followers find themselves in the valley of humiliation. I believe I am fair when I state that it does not lie in the mouths of Liberals to hurl across the floor of this chamber the criticism which they direct against the greatest Canadian and the party supporting him.
I do not know how long this debate will continue. I shall not take up further time.
I sincerely tTust it may soon be completed so that we may defeat the amendment moved by the crown prince from British Columbia and get on with the business of the country. Let us see whether the Liberals will stand true to their promises and to the statement that they are here to support the government and to cooperate in having legislation passed at the earliest possible moment which may bring comfort to those who are suffering from one end of Canada to the other.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since coming to this House of Commons about five yearn ago I have been anxious to cast my vote in support of the most constructive proposals introduced. I have adopted that attitude because in this corner of the house we have no strong party ties. Only on a veiy few occasions do we feel any need for voting together. Taken as a whole I believe the group in this corner of the house have been anxious to give the government an opportunity to put its program into effect as quickly as possible. I believe we

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Maclnnis
indicated that in a similar stand when some time ago we voted against a motion like the present one.
On the present occasion however I feel I must support the amendment, because I believe in substance it states the facts, regardless of the reasons for bringing it forward. I must believe that the motive behind the amendment was the very best possible, and if it comes to a vote I shall vote in favour of it. The amendment states :
This house regrets that notwithstanding the specific promises made prior to the election of 1930 and many times since reiterated, and despite the fact that extraordinary powers to deal with unemployment have been repeatedly secured from parliament, the present administration, after nearly five years of office, has not yet submitted to parliament any definite or effective policy to deal with widespread actual unemployment or distress which continues to be Canada's most urgent national problem.
I think every bon. member, regardless of whether or not he accepts the motion, must agree that the words contained therein are true. Hon. members opposite cannot get away from the fact that undoubtedly they were elected to put an end to unemployment. To-day I heard some of them say, "Well, we have done as well as other countries have done; show us some countries which have done better." They were not elected to do as well as other countries did; they were elected to end unemployment. If we were to accept that answer, then we would have to accept what the Liberals said in 1930,-"Why, conditions *in Canada-are no worse than they are in other countries." That statement would have been as true in 1930 as the statement made by hon. members on the other side to-day. Possibly conditions in other countries are no better than they are in Canada, but we must remember that in 1930 the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) contended that what was true of other countries so far as prevailing conditions were concerned should not and need not be (rue of this country. He said Canada was a young country. Well, to-day we are only a little more than four years older than we Were in 1930, and in the life of a nation four years is a very short time. Speaking in Calgary on June 12, 1930, he said, "This is a new country, and there is no excuse for unemployment in Canada if a government does its duty." If that statement held in 1930 it is just as true to-day.
The hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Stitt) said, "Well, we did make promises in 1930 which we were not able to fulfil, but we did not know that this depression was not similar to former depressions. We thought it would 92582-79
pass away and that everything would be all right." They were depending on Providence to help them carry out their promises, because they have admitted that they did not know anything about the world economic situation.
I have never received the same publicity as the Prime Minister; possibly I have never been entitled to it. To-day however I was looking over the very small amount of publicity I received during the campaign of 1930, and -found that at the first meeting I addressed I said, "The Liberal party is not responsible for the conditions prevailing in Canada today." Let me remind the Liberal party that if they blame this government for the economic conditions prevailing to-day they too are liable to the same accusation, namely that they know nothing about economics. At the same time I made the statement, "The Conservative party will not end unemployment"-and they have not. They could not end unemployment, because unemployment is part of and essential to the capitalistic system. Speaking in this chamber a short time ago the Prime Minister said, "There has always been a certain amount of unemployment in Canada; there has been during the best of times." I am surprised to note how easily he shifts his ground. Speaking in this house on the occasion referred to, he said that in normal times the average unemployment amounted to about 150,000. Speaking during the special session of 1930 he gave an estimate of 117,000 then unemployed, and stated that by the end of December of that year it was anticipated the figure would reach 177,000, if their program did not work out as they expected it would. But despite the fact that he realizes and maintains that the average number of unemployed for some years past was some 150,000-and during the election campaign in 1930 he admitted that the number of the unemployed- was only 117,000-nevertheless he went out on the hustings and said that unemployment had got to the stage where it was a national problem and that the Liberals must be turned out because they had refused to accept it as such. Now you cannot blow hot and cold on these things and get away with it and have the people think you know what you are talking about.
Let me point out to my hon. friends another statement that was made by the Prime Minister. On July 16, speaking at Renfrew, Ontario, he said:
There is no excuse for unemployment in our country. There is no excuse for poverty. We have the people and the resources. We have the capital-

1236	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Maclnnis
But note what follows:
-but the capital will not allow itself to be used unless there is stability and certainty.
Stability and certainty of what? Stability and certainty of profits. Then that denies that we have the things that the Prime Minister said we had. We have the people, we have the resources, we have the capital. Now if we have the resources and the capital surely we can use them to meet the needs of the people of this country. But as a matter of fact the people of this country have not the resources and the capital. The capitalists of this country, the Flavelles, the Holts, the Gordons, the Blacks, and all that gang, those are the people that have the resources of this country, and those are the people that will not allow the resources of this country to be used unless they make a profit out of the process. That is why my friends to my right cannot put an end to unemployment any more than hon. gentlemen opposite without putting an end to the class that is furnishing the funds for the next campaign.
The impossibility of carrying out the promises made by political parties in this country should have become evident to those parties a long time ago. I have always felt that either one of two things must be true with regard to the promises made by the Conservative party during the last election, and particularly by the Prime Minister: either the Conservative party were quite reckless as to what promises they made, or they did not know or understand the conditions with which they were dealing. But whichever it was it does not make any great difference. I believe it was this impossibility of keeping promises made under present conditions that caused the mover of this motion to make the statement in Vancouver some little time ago that he was afraid the Liberals were going to have such a large majority in the next house that it would be difficult to keep them to their promises. I am afraid it will be difficult to keep them to their promises if they make any promises to restore capitalism, or to end unemployment, or to restore trade, or to do any of these things, because they are going to fail just as surely as this government failed to carry out their promises. But the hon. member for Vancouver Centre tried to safeguard at least the British Columbia contingent by saying that they at all events would live up to their promises. So the rest of you gentlemen from the other provinces must realize what they think of you in Vancouver, that you make promises and do not keep them, while the Vancouver contingent does keep its promises.

The conditions in this country to-day have been developing and approaching their present stage for quite a long time. I have in my hand a little pamphlet which has been received I believe by all the members. The title of this little book is Five Years Under Bennett. The author is "Micaw-ber," waiting I presume for something to turn up. Considering who the government is, I suppose that that was the inevitable thing to do. This little pamphlet has rather a Liberal flavour. I am going to quote just a paragraph or two from it to show that if things were not just as bad in 1930 as they are to-day they were bad enough to intimate to the government of that day that something should be done about it. The author of this pamphlet, after drawing attention to what the present government had failed to do, makes this statement:
To wage war against evil everywhere must always be a principal function of any administration. That is not a matter of party policy and Bennett greatly weakens his case when he claims political virtue for deciding to embark upon long overdue reform to clean up the evils of private capitalism which existed and cried aloud for action when he assumed office in 1930.
That is, when the present Prime Minister assumed office in 1930 after nine years of Liberal rule. Yet the evils of private capitalism at the end of that nine years were such that remedies were long overdue and the abuses cried aloud for action.
We have been told, not so much lately, although the statement was made again today, that the unemployed do not want work, or at least that some of them do not. That is something that we might have heard some years ago, but surely we should not hear it at this time. We all admit that there are among the unemployed men who do not wish to work, just as we also know that there are many other people in society who do not wish to work if they can get a living in any other way. But I have before me now a report that was prepared by the relief officer in Vancouver early in 1931, and referring to the men who were unemployed he says:
In the first place the act brought to light the hidden sores of unemployment. Men who were too proud to ask for charity promptly applied for the work they so grievously needed. When the registration of unemployed by the Vancouver city relief department commenced on October 1, crowds of applicants jammed the office, and by November 18, 4,513 married and 5,244 single men had registered. Even this did not represent the total number of unemployed as few clerical workers, union men, seamen and women were on the list.

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Maclnnis
He goes on to say, after referring to one or two people who tried to get something for nothing:
Such cases, however, were far from common. Investigation resulted' in thirty per cent of the married men registrations being placed in the category of "urgent," i.e., needing employment within three weeks to provide the necessities of life.
He continues:
That there is nothing wrong with the unemployed except unemployment holds generally true. At the same time there are exploiters among the jobless equally with every other section of the community.
One of the difficulties that the unemployed are up against is that of getting unemployment relief. I was in a position to put a man who had been on relief some few months ago in Vancouver in touch with a little temporary work, and he refused to do the work. It would have taken only a week or two. He said he had found it so hard and had suffered so much before getting on relief that he did not wish to go through the ordeal again. As a matter of fact they are making it harder all the time for these men to be decent under the trying circumstances with which nearly all of us are confronted. I believe that some one during the debate to-day referred to the fact that the difficult conditions the unemployed were living under were driving them to commit crime. As a matter of fact, in some instances that is the only way in which they can get relief. Let me cite to the house two or three instances out of dozens that I came in contact with during this summer and fall.
A man and his wife called on me early one morning. The man was a returned soldier, a veteran of the great war; he was in ill health; he had been refused a pension, he had three children, which with his wife made a family of five. The affliction or disease from which this man suffered was such that he perspired profusely; yet such were the conditions in his home that they had not a second pair of sheets to change when the others became unsanitary. That is only one of the cases we come across; yet in that home there were three very nice children who were being brought up under such conditions. Again, a lady called on me. Her light had been cut off. They were allowed so much for light but it was not sufficient and the bill was increasing. At last the electric light company, expecting never to be paid their account, cut off the light and these people had to go without any light. They could not get fuel for heating purposes; they were given a small allowance for cooking by gas. And having no fue. for the furnace, when evening came, instead 925S2-791
of putting on a fire as other people do, they had to put on their overcoats or go to bed. Take again the position of the young man under twenty-one in the city of Vancouver. Young people on relief-and there are very many whose parents are not working-are regarded as infants until they reach the age of twenty-one, and for infants the city provides $3.75 a month. Imagine an infant of twenty-one years of age living on $3.75 a month. But that is not the worst; after he has reached the age of twenty-one, there is one of three things he must do; he must either find a job, or go into one of the relief camps, or stay at home and be a burden on the family, who will be minus the $3.75 which he was paid before his twenty-first birthday.
These are circumstances which this government should concern itself with, if the government is concerned with the welfare of the people of Canada. I believe the conditions in Vancouver are generally speaking just as good as, if not better, than they are in most other cities in Canada. I have here a clipping from the Montreal Daily Herald of February 7 in which there appears an interview with E. J. Lincoln, executive head of the Golden Rule Association. The interview is to the effect that welfare groups, companies and individuals had promised sufficient support to repair certain quarters to provide a shelter for homeless men on relief, but they were not able to get permission from the city to open this shelter, the city officials taking the view that the shelter would prove an attraction to jobless people outside the municipalities, and that such a gathering place would become the centre of red propaganda. Mr. Lincoln goes on to say:	.
Despite the statement of Albert Chevalier, director of the Meurling refuge, to the contrary. I guarantee that there are between 1,500 and 2,000 homeless men in the city at present, most of whom will do almost anything, the least of which is to seek nightly shelter in police stations to save them from lodging at the Meurling refuge where the rules are ridiculously severe. The inmates of the Meurling refuge are treated like unruly animals; they are not allowed to exchange one word from the time they enter at 6.30 p.m. until they are evicted at 7 a.m.
They are not allowed to stay in the refuge during the day; they must go into the streets in their flimsy rags and endure the cold. Surely any government that is sympathetic to the people must pay some attention to conditions such as these. My hon. friends on the government side declare that they are just as sympathetic as we are, but you have to have something more than sympathy;
1238	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Maclnnis
sympathy without action is of little value.
I submit that there is a sufficiency of everything necessary in this country. The Prime Minister himself admitted this in the city of Kingston a few days ago, when he said that we had everything necessary to give a full life to everyone. If that is so I would ask this government, if it is a government, why it does not do something to bring this condition about. As I look at the various monuments standing on the grounds on parliament hill I often wonder whether the time will ever come when I shall see a monument to the Prime Minister and one to the Leader of the Opposition. I believe there is every reason why there should be monuments to both. We might put up a monument to the Leader of the Opposition for reforming the Senate and a monument to the Prime Minister for ending unemployment.

Why not one to

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, we can do that
too. I am supporting the motion moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre because I believe it deserves the support of this house. But I confess that, although the hon. gentleman is a member of a party which, in his own words, expects to be back as a government with strong support, I cannot see why he has not put forward something for the party as a whole. He has put forward certain views of his own, but I should like to know why, as one who is likely to be in the next cabinet, he cannot advance something that represents the views of his party. Why did he not confer with his leader and put forward something which we could defi-'nitely support? There were one or two things that struck me in the proposals he made. Take the second one:
I want to advocate the handling of this entire problem as one of national emergency, even if only for a limited time, until this depression is over.
But does he think this depression will be over within a limited time? If so, on what ground does he base that opinion? Let me again remind him of the statement made by the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Stitt) to-day that in 1930 they thought the depression would be over in a short while and that as soon as they got into office they would be able to handle it easily. Let me tell my hon. friend that there is no indication the depression will be over within a limited time. The depression is here to stay as long as we hold to the capitalistic system. Then he says:

I suggest adequate, immediate and effective measures to increase our domestic and foreign trade.
What are the adequate, immediate and effective measures that are going to increase trade? I would like to know what they are. The only way in which trade can be increased in my opinion is by increasing the purchasing power of the great mass of the people, the farmer, the industrial worker; but if you increase the purchasing power of the farmer and the industrial worker, you decrease the profits of the employing class. You have here a certain amount of production; suppose it is divided equally now, so much going to each side; you cannot divide it in any other way without giving one party either more or less than the other. If you are going to give the workers and farmers more, you will have to give the employer class less, and just because you must do that, under the profit system you are going to have those who live by interest and profit against you all the time. Until you reach the stage where you are stronger, where you can do things without having regard to those people you are not going to improve trade, end unemployment or increase the living standard of the Canadian people.
In the program that has been brought down so far there is nothing that will improve the position of the working class or the farmer in any appreciable way within at least the next two years. Therefore, while I am supporting the motion and think it is justified in every respect, I wish the mover of it had gone somewhat further than he has and had explained to us how the Liberal party proposes to improve the position of those at present in need. How are they going to get the workers out of relief camps? How are they going to get the thousands of men who are on relief, the 1,200,000 or so that the hon. gentleman mentioned, placed in a position where they can provide for themselves? I claim that under the present system this cannot be done, and when we suggest that it can be done we are only fooling the people and ourselves.

I too regret that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) did not tell ^ us what in his opinion, his personal opinion, could be done to get these workingmen out of the relief camps. I further regret that the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis) followed the bad example of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre and did not inform us how he would get the workers out of the relief camps, except to suggest that

Unemployment Reliej-Mr. Turnbull
he would change the system; but he did not tell us how the system, when he got it changed, would do this.

speechtext: We are still waiting.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member says: "We are still waiting." It is true hon. gentlemen opposite express a great deal of sympathy with the condition in which unfortunate people in this country find themselves. It is also true that there is sympathy extended toward those people by every person in Canada and out of it. I do not blame hon. members opposite for talking about the sympathy end of the matter because that is the only end they have to talk about. When they tell about their sympathies, they have exhausted themselves.
The motion before the house is as usual a negative one; it merely expresses regret that the government did not do something, but it does not express any views as to what the government ought to do, or as to what the opposition would do, or even as to the personal views of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. That is quite in line with the tactics pursued by the Liberal party for the last four or five years. I would not like to go so far as to say that they are animated by political motives, but I might point out that they are following pretty closely the program set forth by the present Premier of Ontario in 1930 when he said, as reported at page 1886 of Hansard of that year:
As I say, we are going to settle the unrest among the farmers, the unrest which has been created because of an economic disturbance which is world wide. I refer to the question of overproduction. When we have overproduction it is always followed by a period of low prices, and in a period of low prices it is very easy to stir up trouble, especially in the rural sections.
I suggest that the Liberal party are only running true to form; they are doing exactly what Mr. Hepburn in 1930 advised them to do, what they have been doing for the last five years and what they will do for the next five yearn whether they return to parliament on the opposition or the government side. Of course it is easy to find fault. According to Robert West, nothing is easier than fault finding. No talent, no self denial, no brains, no character are required to set up in the grumbling business.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) a few days ago read us a homily in. the house because a resolution introduced on this side was according to him a political one. That served him as an excuse to vote Liberal, to exercise the
innate liberalism which he has always possessed, coupled with a thin veneer of cooperative commonwealth federation. To-day a similar motion, just as political as the other, is introduced from the other side, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and his following have found an excuse for again voting Liberal, just as they did during the last five years of Liberal rule. If there is anything the Liberals did that they should not have done between 1926 and 1930, the blame rests as much at the door of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as it does at the door of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), because the former is the man above all -men who, according to his own statement, with his confrere from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), maintained the former Liberal government in office from 1926 to 1930.

speechtext: Will the hon. member state why he and the whole Conservative party voted with us for a similar motion in 1930?

speechtext: It is very easy to do that. In 1930 there was a motion that something foe done about unemployment. At that time nothing was done, nothing was being done. The leader of the opposition was declaring that he would not distribute any unemployment relief except on a political basis; that he had not a five cent piece for any province that was not Liberal; that no Conservative province would get any money. But conditions are entirely different to-day. Something is being done for unemployment every day the house sits and every day of the week between the time the house prorogues and the opening of the next session. That is why hon. members on this side voted for a similar resolution in 1930 and are voting against the present one to-day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman will concede that Labour members at that time voted against the Liberals, as to-day they are voting against the Conservatives.

speechtext:
This amendment, while it is accompanied by a great deal of language regarding the distressing condition . of the unemployed, as to which we all agree, nevertheless if carried would have the effect of preventing this government from doing anything for the unemployed until after another election. Hon. members who profess to be in favour of social reform, to believe in all these things in principle, but who oppose them
1240	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Turnbull
in practice when they have the chance, would if this resolution carried dismiss this government without anything being done along the lines of the legislation of which they profess to be so strongly in favour. Yet the hon. member for Vancouver Centre talks of "oleaginous hyprocrisy," and his leader goes back and forth through the country talking of the hypocrisy of Hon. H. H. Stevens in connection with the price spreads and mass buying investigation. I leave it to this house and to the country to say where the hypocrisy comes in.
I read with some amazement the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. It was amazing for some of the statements contained in it; it was amazing in view of the position he hoped to attain in the Liberal party. I thought for a moment it was the rising star of the white hope of the Vancouver Sun dawning on the horizon. But, evidently feeling the cold blast coming from the seat diagonally forward of him, he changed his tone and said he was not speaking for the Liberal party but expressing only his personal feelings. So the comet that flashed across the horizon vanished in gas and hot air as comets usually do. At one part of his speech the hon. member for Vancouver Centre made the statement that Canada had led the world in the march towards higher tariffs-an amazing statement. The hon. member must realize that there was not a year between 1926 and 1930 that tariffs were not going higher in every country except possibly Canada. And if Canada was leading the march towards higher tariffs it must have started five years before we came into office, because the march was well under way in 1926, and in 1930 the Liberal party joined in the march, because the Dunning budget increased the tariff on more articles than did the treaties with Great Britain.
I suggest to hon. members opposite that if they will allow the government to go into supply the probabilities are that in due course the government's legislation with regard to unemployment relief will come dowm. But that is what they are afraid of; they would rather discuss it on an abstract basis, with no measure before them, than on a concrete basis. They are still theorizers; they are prepared to discuss anything but facts. They will discuss principles from morning to night, but something concrete to put these principles into effect is beyond their horizon. All these things they say are objectives of the Liberal party. The other day the leader of the opposition told us free trade in automobiles was an objective of the Liberal party. I do not know how many years it has been their

objective. If they were in office I do not know how many years it would continue to be their objective, but I suggest that objectives cease to be objectives when they have been reached, and the Liberal party never reach their objectives so long as they can use them to get votes.
Another amazing statement of the hon. member was that this government put a bonus on wheat restriction. He did not tell us where or when or how, in all probability because he did not know; for they did not do it.

That seems fairly

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
A very prominent member on the other side of the house, a man who occupied a cabinet position in the former government, who was Minister of Agriculture, and who comes from western Canada and therefore should be acquainted with the wheat situation, was one of those who most prominently urged restriction, of wheat production. If hon. gentlemen will turn to Hansard for the session of 1932-33 they will find these words credited1 to the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) at page 991:
Whether or not we like it, our wheat production must be reduced to near the world's capacity to consume. Otherwise the situation will continue to get worse and worse. Our carryover is becoming larger each year. I recognize the fact that no one country could afford to reduce its wheat acreage without similar action being taken by the others.
Then after condemning us because we had so treated Russia that we could not get an agreement with her, according to the hon. gentleman, he said:
Are we going to go along blindly until we become so impoverished that many farmers will not have the equipment or strength with which to put in a crop? That will be the result of the ruthless law of the survival of the fittest.
I did not hear any dissenting voice from the hon. member for Vancouver Centre when his confrere in the former government declared that wheat production should be restricted, but to-day in opposition he raises a bogy that does not exist and says this government bonused wheat restriction.
Another amazing statement of the hon. member was that this government put the people of this country on the dole. This government never put people on the dole. The only reason why direct relief is in force in Canada is that the provinces came to the federal government and said they, were no longer able to bear their share of indirect relief, and they asked this government-they whose duty it was to administer relief-to

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Turnbull
do it in the form of direct relief and not in the form of employment of labour. May I say in passing, that when the hon. member for Vancouver South, refers to the way in which the unemployed were treated in Montreal he should carry his complaints not to this government, which has nothing to do with the administration of unemployment relief, but either to the province of Quebec or to the city of Montreal, which have to do with these things in that vicinity. I do not know what purpose is served by cataloguing lists of people who have suffered hardship. I do not know of a time in the history of this country when some people did not suffer hardships. I could give case after case of people who have been run over by railway trains or have been hungiy or who have not had all the clothing they needed for their beds. But to show a situation does not provide a remedy.
Another statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre was that this government had raised the tariff in 1930 before going to the imperial conference for the purpose of negotiating treaties in the fall of that year. I heard the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) say the other day that when the motion to put these tariff increases in effect was put to this house he was the only man who opposed it, by saying, "On division." There might have been one or two others, but he apparently expressed the view that the rest of the members on the other side had concurred in the raising of these tariffs in 1930. Indeed there was no reason why they should not, because they themselves had raised them on many articles in the Dunning budget a few short months before.
I want to deal for a short time with at least some of the personal views of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. I feel that the leader of the opposition must have breathed much more freely when he heard the hon. member for Vancouver Centre say he was not committing his nominal leader by the views he expressed in the house. Nothing could be said on this side that would have been a more masterly condemnation of the policy of inactivity and laissez-faire of the Liberal party than those views expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre last night.
But let us examine some of his proposed remedies. The first was a national relief commission, and the second was that the problem of relief should be handled as a national emergency. I cannot see much difference between the two. He was following his
leader in that regard, and this in spite of the fact that his leader and he both know perfectly well that the provinces will never consent to that method of handling relief. Consequently that can remain an objective of the Liberal party and perhaps serve some good purpose during the election campaign. In the campaign of 1926 the right hon. leader of the opposition addressed certain meetings in the province of Saskatchewan at which he preached the doctrine of a solid Saskatchewan and a solid Quebec, while some place else his friend the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was preaching unity. A solid Saskatchewan and a solid Quebec was what the Liberals relied upon at that time to put them 'back in office, and it served the purpose very well, because then we did not have a national system of radio. If the Liberal party intend to get back into power in 1935, once more it will be through the solid Saskatchewan, and the solid Quebec, so let us see the attitude of these two provinces in respect of this national relief commission. Mr. Tasohereau is on record as declaring that he will not allow the dominion government to administer relief within the boundaries of his province. He is quite prepared to accept dominion money which he can spend, but so far as letting the dominion government spend it, that is quite beyond any idea Mr. Tas-chereau ever had.

Your proposals for dealing with relief situation in drought areas do not commend them-

speechtext: Lower the tariff.
