speechtext:
That is a bright idea.
If we spend less money we are told to spend more. If we raise the taxes we are told to lower them again. In his speech the hon. member stated he wanted us to balance the budget, but in the same speech he advocated that the responsibility for relief should be shouldered by the dominion and taken from the provinces and municipalities. Will that help us balance the budget? Then he advocated public works. How can we spend money on public works and still balance our budget? Next he suggested that we should assist private companies. There is 'no limit to the amount of money which could be spent in assisting private companies. When private individuals get government money to spend, the government has not a very good guarantee of getting that money back. That has been the history of government assistance to private institutions as far back as I can remember.
Then he offered a suggestion which may have a good deal of merit in it, although certainly it would not help to balance the budget. His proposal was an "extension of the principle of the War Veterans' Allowance Act, by reducing the age to fifty-five years." In short, the proposition of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre is to spend money in new and additional ways, in huge amounts, so as to relieve unemployment, and at the same time to balance the budget. To be able to accomplish that end one would need to be as great an acrobat in financial matters as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre is in the use of language.
Then, proposition number eleven is a financial conference with the provinces "to consider the advisability of establishing a national loan board to coordinate, if possible, the investment activities of governments," and so on. This is to be a financial conference with the provinces to consider a national board to be set up to control provincial expenditures. How far would the hon. member get with Mr. Pattullo on that point? How quickly would Mr. Pattullo, who is opposed to any amendment to the British North America Act, agree to have his finances controlled by a national board? How about Mr. Taschereau, who states there will be no amendment to the British North
1244	COMMONS
Unemployment Reliej-Mr. Turnbull
America Act? Where would the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) stand, the man who declares that Quebec will fight to the last ditch any amendments to the British North America Act? How far would he agree to a national board to oversee expenditures of the province of Quebec? In the days when the provinces and the municipalities were doubling, trebling, quadrupling their expenditures, why did not the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, or the members of his party, institute a national board and lock the door before the horse was stolen? Why did he not have a national board set up to prevent the provinces and municipalities from going into debt and increasing their expenditures each year the Liberal government was in office? Why is he so keen to have some control effected after the damage is done? His proposition I submit is impracticable, because the provinces would not agree to it.
His twelfth proposition, the one respecting the War Veterans' Allowance Act, is the one with which I must have a great deal of sympathy. The burned out soldier loses his ability much earlier than seventy years of age; he is probably as old at sixty as the average man at seventy. The War Veterans' Allowance Act might very well be amended so as to apply to returned soldiers at an earlier age than seventy.
Then the hon. member wound up his speech with the unlucky thirteenth item. He did not put the number on it, because that might have looked bad. But as a thirteenth item in this great program of reconstruction, in which he has set forth his personal views and not the views of his party, he quoted a paragraph from the book-a paragraph from Industry and Humanity. It is full of language, full of expression and full also of inaction. It is a book which remained a book from 1918 to 1934, a book which was hidden up on the shelves; its author had forgotten where he put it. It was never brought out and used. There is a story which reveals why the 1919 Liberal platform was not put into effect. There is a reason why that was not done. That arose as a result of the election in 1921. If the right hon. leader of the opposition would tell the story of what took place in the few months after that election; if he would tell of the men from Montreal who interviewed him within a few months of the election; if he would tell the story of the thumb that was put upon his back and that kept him in a state of inaction for the next nine years, history would know that the Liberal party was the party of laissez-faire because it had to be.

speechtext:
If he does not remember it, some of his friends in the Progressive party may be able to tell him some day.
May I close by stating that if hon. gentlemen opposite are as anxious to make progress during this session, as they say they are; if they are anxious to proceed with legislation in an orderly manner, as they say they are; if they are anxious to have social reforms placed upon the statute books of this country, as they say they are, then it is pretty hard to believe they are sincere in view of the fact that their conversion has been so recent. If they are so anxious to conclude the present session, then they will cease making amendments such as the one we are now discussing, amendments which have only the effect of preventing the house from doing business. If accepted, the amendment would prevent the house from doing any further business, because it is a motion of want of confidence, and at the same time and by the same token it is a vote of confidence in the Liberal party; because if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Vancouver South vote for this motion they vote to defeat the government, a government which is doing something for the people of Canada, and to place in power in Ottawa a party which has done nothing for them. That is the alternative which hon. gentlemen must face. They cannot vote for this resolution and for the defeat of this government without at the same time voting for the policy of laissez-faire which they themselves have condemned in no uncertain terms. If they do vote for the Liberal party-or, to be more precise, for the personal views expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre-then they vote in condemnation of all they have said in this chamber about the Liberal party either at this session or the last.
So far as I am concerned I should prefer to see the opposition abandon its blockading tactics and allow the government to proceed with the business of the country. I have not the slightest doubt that in the course of time the government will introduce legislation at

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Luchkovich
the present session, as it has done in other sessions, to take care of the unemployed. Hon. gentlemen opposite know perfectly well that upon such occasion they will have ample opportunity to discuss anything they may wish to discuss concerning unemployment. But they would rather have the people believe that the Liberal party has been responsible for bringing forward the idea of taking care of the unemployed, and they do not wish to be placed in the position of having to discuss measures which in due course the government will introduce. In my judgment the resolution is purely political, and it passes my knowledge how hon. members of this house can vote against a resolution brought in by one party on the basis of its being political, and then vote for an equally political resolution just because it is brought in by the other party, unless there is something in their minds that they were not entirely able to eradicate when they joined the new movement.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, nine long years ago I entered the house an innocent and guileless man, politically speaking, but after the lapse of that time I must unfortunately confess that I have lost a lot of that original innocence and that original guilelessness. Members of this group find themselves very much between the devil and the deep blue sea so far as this resolution is concerned. We find ourselves between the upper and nether millstones ready to be ground into dust by either one or the other of the two parties.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Does the hon. member suggest that the blue sea is on this side?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, I do not know that the blue sea is over there, but I do know that on this question of the unemployed a good many of us are at sea. The hon. member who introduced this resolution (Mr. Mackenzie) is somewhat like the pied piper: he is trying to chase all the metaphorical rats in the Conservative program down into the Ottawa river. He says that he and his small group of British Columbia members are going to come down here somewhat like the band of Spartans that fought off the Persian hordes at Thermopylae. There is this difference, however, that the Spartan band was successful, but we do not know yet whether the British Columbia band of mountaineers will be equally successful.
The hon. member said that the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) had a deathbed conversion, that like Paul's conversion on the way to Damascus Mr. Bennett was converted
before the next election. It does seem to me that the official opposition has not been converted to any reform at all yet, judging by the speeches that have been delivered on this resolution. They used to tell me as a little boy that unless you confessed your sins you were liable to go to the hot place, and it may be that unless there is that conversion on the part of the official opposition they also may be bound for that so-called nether region at the next election.
I have read this resolution carefully, and it is very similar to a resolution that was introduced into this house in 1930 by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). On that occasion when the division came there were 81 yeas and 100 nays, the Conservatives voting with this group for the resolution, but when the vote is taken on the amendment now before the house I imagine that the Liberals and this small group will vote for the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie).
After hearing so many speeches on unemployment I would like to ask this question: What is the difference between the Conservative party and the Liberal party, not only on the unemployment problem but so far as the tariff issue and all other issues are concerned? I frankly confess that both parties are going to use the issue of the tariff at the next election. On the one hand we shall hear the Conservatives say that they will make high tariffs fight for us, and on the other hand we shall hear the Liberals say that they will make low tariffs fight for us. It is true that the government of the day did raise the tariff, as they promised to do. I am not a believer in high tariffs, but I do not believe that the Liberals in the past have lowered the tariff as much as they have professed to do, not only during the past parliament but during other sessions when in power. That lack of difference between the two parties in regard to all these issues has brought a little ditty to my mind which runs as follows:
Says Tweedledum to Tweedledee,
Resign and give your place to me;
Says Tweedledee to Tweedledum,
If they want you they must be dumb;
For the moral in this little ditty,
Taught by men both wdse and witty,
The Conservative Ins, the Liberal Outs, They take the public for a bunch of louts; They promise this and they promise that But they all strike out when they come to bat;
The Liberal Outs, the Conservative Ins,
Are merely two Canadian Siamese twins.
I have already referred to a resolution in essence similar to the one now before the house, introduced on March 31, 1930, by the
1246	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Luchkovich
hon. member lor North Winnipeg. On that occasion what did the Liberal opposition have to say? I have here the speech of the present leader of the opposition. He said:
Let me repeat that statement. I can see nothing arising out of a recognition of this problem as a national problem which obliges this federal government, having regard to our constitution and the division of powers under it, to collect taxes from the people generally in order to meet a situation which affects only a certain group of people in some municipalities in this country, but which does not adversely affect the country as a whole. I am not saying we could not do such a thing; I am not saying that this federal parliament cannot vote money for any purposes for which it may desire so to do, but I am trying to make it clear that under our constitution I do not think it was ever intended that this federal government should become the agency through which problems which are primarily municipal and provincial should be dealt with.
In 1930 it was stated by the leader of the Liberal opposition that this was a municipal and provincial matter, but here we have the hon. member for Vancouver Centre introducing a resolution condemning this government for not doing anything about unemployment, after his own leader had said that the problem of unemployment was a provincial and municipal matter. The leader of the opposition further said:
Employment is a matter of contract and civil rights.
Further on he said:
... how little we have a national problem of unemployment in this country at the present time.
And at page 1227 he says this:
But I would not give a single cent to any Tory government.
And further on he said that if he called a , conference of provincial premiers on unemployment, foreign countries would hesitate to make investments in Canada. In other words, he did not wish to inaugurate any system of getting out of this unemployment situation because he thought that by doing so foreign investments would be driven out of the country.
Listening to the speeches of some members on the other side one is led to believe that in view of the stand pat tendencies of the official opposition those hon. gentlemen, in asking for the resignation of the government at the present time, could base their argument only on the assumption that it had been proved that the present government lacks the confidence of the people, that it lacks a policy, and that the official opposition has a policy which is better than anything that the government in power has done.
'Mr. Luchkovich.]
Now, it is not for me to defend the policy of the government; let the government do that for themselves. I voted for the trade pacts in 1932 because I felt at the time that that was one of the only measures in sight to get us out of the present mess in which we find ourselves. I do not think that the trade pacts are as good as the party in power would have us believe, nor do I think they are as bad as the official opposition suggests. But I did think they were one way of getting, out of the depression, and that is the reason I voted for them. As regards the hon. member who has moved this resolution, if he asks for the resignation of the government without offering an alternative policy of his own, he is placing himself not only in an untenable position but in a position that is ridiculous as well. He is very much in the position of the polar bear mentioned by Lloyd George in his speech-a bear perched on an iceberg which is rapidly melting away as it approaches the equator. Without a substitutive remedy his resolution loses much of its force. It may be good politics to rely on the prevalent discontent throughout the country, but it is folly to ask for the resignation of one government and the return of another without offering some remedy as a substitute. It is folly to put one party out and another in merely because we like the way the leader of the opposition combs his hair better than the manner in which the Prime Minister brushes his. Someone says that neither has any; that makes it still worse.

At any rate I hope
hon. members will accept my address as one that is spoken with the utmost sincerity. I have been asked by many people in the west what difference there is between the two parties. Not long ago an article appeared in Canadian Business, written I think by Leslie Roberts, who says that ever since confederation there have been only three fundamental differences between the two parties; in 1911 reciprocity, in 1917 conscription and in 1926 the constitutional issue. At the present time it would appear that even the Prime Minister is just as anxious to have reciprocity with the United States as is the leader of the opposition; as regards conscription, that to-day, is a dead issue; and as regards the constitutional question of 1926, that also is a thing of the past in so far as it was used then for political purposes. That there-

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Luchkovich
fore reduces the fundamental differences to nil because there are no differences, no fundamental differences to-day. I feel in my hearts

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: No heart.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
No heart? Well, the hon. gentleman has monopolized the hearts of this house and possibly I have none. It was prophesied by the dean and the seer of the house that the Liberals would be the next government in Canada, but in my opinion unless the leader of the opposition comes out flat-footed and puts a definite policy before the Canadian people so that they can judge for themselves as to the differences between the two parties, then the same fate will befall the opposition that has been predicted for the present government. Unless that alternative policy is presented to the people I see no point in the substitution of one party for another; and if that alternative policy cannot be supplied, then why should the people be asked to jump from the frying pan into the fire? It may be good strategy to base one's politics on the expediency of the moment and to maintain a sphinx-like attitude in face of the depression and also to bank on the public dissatisfaction with the government in order to regain power, as well as on a lucky break in the economic tide to retain oneself therein. But I feel that the party seeking power in future will not get very far with any evasive strategy of that sort. Unless an alternative is placed squarely before the people, a definite N.R.A. policy, I have no doubt that the official opposition will meet with the fate that the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) has prophesied for the government. On more than one occasion I have heard it said throughout Canada that the present leader of the opposition does not need a policy to get into power because public dislike of t'he government will put him back. That may be so, but it most certainly will not keep him in power. Unless he evolves a more genuine and practical policy, more practical than anything enunciated in this house either during this session or in past sessions, I am. afraid that his characteristic vacillation will strike the death blow to parliamentarism as we know it to-day. By seeking office without offering a substitutive remedy, he is virtually putting himself "on the spot," and in view of the recent pronouncements of the Prime Minister in regard to the new order and in regard to reform, I do not think the leader of the opposition can afford to play the old stereotyped battle of the Ins and the Outs and the Tweedtedums and Tweedledees, or to wait
for Providence to help him out in this miserable game of politics, because in the future I am not so sure that as Sir Wilfrid Laurier used to say Providence will be on the side of the Liberal party.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: 'It always has been.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, there is a new rule now to be enacted called "God helps those who help themselves," this does not mean easy campaign funds but plain hard honest application by the people and the government, and I am afraid the Liberals have not at least at the present time such a policy. In the past it seems to me-and I speak in all sincerity-that the Liberals have been sponging a little bit too much on the Almighty, but in the future it does not look as though they will be able to get away with it; for Providence has mode that road much harder and the obstacles and hindrances placed thereon much more difficult to remove. I cannot conceive of the laissez-faires tackling a job that will require so much work, but if they do, then I expect their avoirdupois will greatly decrease within the next few years if in the meantime the reducing process does not actually kill them.
Much has been said about government intervention. I believe in a certain amount of it. The birth of a new order has made government intervention obligatory. I wonder how many members of the official opposition really realize what they are in for when they become the next government; for if they do not, then one must conclude with the words of the poet that "where ignorance is bliss, 'tis folly to be wise."

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member is a living illustration.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Hanbury) has given us a living illustration. He should be the last man to make a statement of that kind. I see him strutting in his seat over there. I have seen men strut while they stand up, strut while they walk, and strut while they dance, but he is the best example I know of any man being able to strut so ostensibly even while he is sitting down. As far as the official opposition are concerned they have done nothing nor said anything this session that would lead one to believe they were actually going to march forward toward their professed goal of reform. It is the same old story about tariffs, finding new markets and restoring old ones.
I was quite amused during the dying hours of last session to hear the hon. member for
1248	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Luchkovich
South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) twitting the members on the government side and also this group about the next election, how our heads would roll into the trough of political oblivion, and how he tried to put fear into our followers throughout the country. Greatly encouraged by recent provincial victories, this grizzly old warrior started to decapitate all and sundry in the house. Even the leader of the opposition on that occasion was not free from this somewhat bloodthirsty attitude, and time and again he would emerge with club in hand to obliterate the big, bad Prime Minister over yonder and his retinue behind him.
So far as I am concerned I might take seriously the challenge in this resolution were it not for the lack of an alternative policy on the part of the hurlers. What does the resolution mean? Strange as this may seem, I intend to vote for the resolution. In view of the fact that we voted for a similar resolution in 1930, it logically follows that we must again vote for a similar one now. But I say that simply routing one form of conservatism and substituting another for it will get us nowhere. As for restoring old markets and finding new ones, I still remember the Fordney-McCumber and the Hawley-Smoot bills passed in the United States, which in 1929 killed our trade with that country in so far as agricultural products and lumber are concerned, as well as the various quota restrictions and impositions that have been placed against our exports to the European market.
The other day the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) waxed very indignant when I made certain metaphorical comments on the free trade speeches of certain Liberal lieutenants in and out of the house. References were made to the extravagant expectations aroused by this oratory, the purpose of which was to create throughout this country the impression that this fair dominion would blossom as the rose and be with milk and honey blessed, and that tyrants throughout the whole world would cringe in fear once it was learned that the present opposition was returned to power. Visions were conjured up of an irate populace threatened by five years of misrule attacking the bastile of special privilege, singing the deathknell of protection to the tune of the author, the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) and of a revengeful public enraged by loss of markets marching round the walls of Jericho not once but seven times-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: With trumpets.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
-yes, until the
trumpets from Temiscouata, the promulgation of the 1935 Liberal free trade policy and the acid pulverizing negotiating power of the king of Prince Albert caused the mighty rocks to crumble like sandstone in an avalanche, with a grateful electorate proclaiming their timely deliverance and the king of Prince Albert adjuring them at the time, saying: "Cursed be he before the Lord who riseth and buildeth up the tariff walls of Jericho. He shall be put to the sword, just as we killed all the other Tories within the walls of the former Jericho. And the Lord was with the king of Prince Albert, and his fame was noised abroad throughout the length and breadth of the land." Such were the visions conjured up by certain hon. members not only in this house but also throughout the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
This is a caveman's
speech.

speechtext:
I imagine the hon.
member for Temiscouata thinks the Canadian people should now be of good cheer; for the litter will soon be refilled and our pockets will jingle again;, the lowing kine and the bleating sheep and the grunting pigs will soon fill the empty freight cars and will proceed by the hundreds of thousands to the markets of the world as aforetime.

speechtext:
Don't forget the golden
calf.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall not forget
the bellowing calf from Temiscouata.
Such is the dream, but what is the reality? I do not propose to set myself up, as the hon. member for Temiscouata seems to think, as a U.FA. Mark Antony either to praise or to bury the right hon. gentleman who heads this government, for, as Shakespeare said, the evil that men do lives after them; the good is oft interred with their bones; so let it be with the Prime Minister. But I do ask the leader of the opposition what he would do if he were in the Prime Minister's place. I think the country has a right to know. They will not be satisfied with the present negative attitude of the Liberal party, nor are they in a humour for the old gag, "We shall not prescribe until we are called in." On many occasions I have heard the leader of the opposition say that the Prime Minister was an autocrat. If that were so it were a grievous fault, and grievously the Prime Minister will have to answer for it. But again I say that the people have a right to know what the leader of the opposition

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Hackett
would do if he were in the Prime Minister's place. This rowing with muffled oars to his objective may be all right, but the people want to know what he is going to do when he gets there.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Something that you can't understand.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
Again there is the
loud sound that speaks the vacant mind.
We want to know what they are going to do to put purchasing power in the pockets of the people, what they are going to do to raise the price of primary products, to cure unemployment and to control the country's finances and banking facilities. We heard them say throughout Canada: If we are returned to power we are going to nationalize the banks; yet when a resolution was brought up in this house to nationalize the banks some hon. members said: Yes, we want to nationalize the central bank, but not the other banks. It is like the lady who wrote to the paper saying a certain thing resembled a man trying to learn to swim with one foot in the water and the other on the land. It simply can't be done. If you are going to nationalize the central bank you have to nationalize the other banks as well; but when that resolution came up for a vote there was a mad dash on the part of the official opposition to the narrow aperture that leads to the lobby. Many of them were almost killed in the rush, and it was noticed that those who spoke so vociferously in favour of nationalizing the banks were conspicuous by their absence when the reso-tion came to a vote.
Now it has been said that the hon. member who introduced this banking resolution last year introduced a tripartite amendment of alphabetical stupidity to the central bank bill. He wanted a bill for a central bank that was (a) controlled and owned nationally, (b) government owned, or (c) government controlled. This resolution must have been offered with the feeling that it might be heaven, hell or purgatory his party might share so they thought it well to make friends everywhere. I noticed in the speech he made on the amendment to the motion to go into supply that he very cautiously left out the whole subject of finance and the banks, which of course is the pivotal point, the main thing. You have to reform your finances before you start reforming anything else, and once they are reformed all the other things will take care of themselves. The policy of this group is a program of useful social services financed out of the
real credit of the country without incurring interest or debt. Sooner or later that will involve the nationalization not only of our central bank but of our whole banking system. That is the alternative policy of this group, and certainly it is a better alternative than the policy produced here by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre.
As I have already said I intend to vote for this amendment of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre because it is very much like the resolution introduced by the hon. member for North Winnipeg in 1930. It is not a nice position to be, as I said, between the devil and the deep blue sea, but there is no other way out for us. So I for one intend to vote for the resolution, not because of what the hon. member for Vancouver Centre has said concerning their futile alternative policy, but because we voted for the same thing in 1930, and logically we must do it now.

Question.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Why so much haste to put the question? Who started this discussion?
I have followed the progress of this debate and have been amazed, in reading the proposed amendment, to see that while the aim of the hon. gentleman who introduced it avowedly was to give the house the benefit of his wisdom in discovering and applying some means that would dispel unemployment, he quite forgot to say what they were. The members of a very learned body assembled the other day for the purpose of discovering some solution for the railway problem. They passed a resolution and sent it to various hon. members. In it they called upon the government to see that effective measures were taken to solve the railway problem. That is about as definite as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) was in his speech. I noticed how warmly the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Riinfret) acclaimed the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre that all immigration barriers should be torn down and that we should welcome to this country all and sundry who might wish to come.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
However it is not my purpose to endeavour to follow the hon. gentleman in the different statements he made last evening. He purported to be very much interested in unemployment, of course everyone in the house is interested in that problem. Unemployment is localized; it is to be found in the big cities of the dominion. Outside of the cities there is no unemployment that is extraordinary or need cause worry to any person. If by any chance the cities of Montreal, Toronto, Ottawa, Hamilton, Winnipeg, Vancouver and possibly Calgary were moved 'beyond our borders tonight we would have no unemployment problem in the dominion to-morrow morning. It is in the industrial life of the country that unemployment exists. It is because large and ever growing numbers have been taken from other vocations, particular from that of tilling the soil, that we now have this loss of equilibrium which expresses itself in large, apparently indissoluble lumps of humanity incapable, in their present situation, of providing for themselves and their families. In no province is this problem more pronounced than in the province of Quebec. In no province has the trek from the land to the city been as rapid or as continuous. In no province is the percentage of people on the land so small. To-day barely a third of the people of the province1 of Quebec is engaged in tilling the soil.
If we cannot, devise some means of finding markets for the products of our industrial establishments we must admit that the possibility of gainful employment for people in the city is remote. The work which these people flocked to the cities to do was not work which resulted from prosperous or

voluminous external trade. In large measure the work which they came to do was work which resulted from the policy of expansion and borrowing which characterized the last decade. To-day we find that cities, municipalities and provinces are heavily indebted, and it was during the period that they were spending the money they borrowed that great industrial activity occurred. I remember one day hearing the late Sir Henry Thornton say that he had built freight cars in numbers sufficient if placed end to end to reach from the city of Montreal to the city of Kitchener. It was while we were carrying on work of that kind, constructing machinery, constructing tools and implements for use in the building of roads, building telephone lines and storage dams and equipping ourselves to supply and serve a population of twenty million or twenty-five million people, when we were making these improvements many of which need never be renewed, that for a few years we found employment in the cities for people who hitherto had been engaged on the soil.
On motion of Mr. Hackett the debate was adjourned.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Wednesday, February 27, 1935
